title: Clinical and functional outcomes of aquatic plyometrics in adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome: a dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Optimal management of adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome requires evidence-based interventions that maximize physical recovery without overloading the patellofemoral joint. This study investigated the efficacy of aquatic plyometric (Aquatic-Plyo) exercises on pain, muscle strength, and functional disability and health-related quality of life in this demographic.
DESIGN: A dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
SUBJECTS/PATIENTS: 56 adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome (age: 10-18 years).
METHODS: Adolescents were allocated to an experimental Aquatic-Plyo group or a control group performing conventional exercises. Both arms completed 45-min sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks. Pre- and post-treatment assessments included pain intensity, isokinetic knee (quadriceps and hamstrings) torque at 120°/s and 180°/s, functional disability, and health-related quality of life.
RESULTS: Mixed-model ANOVA confirmed the therapeutic dominance of the Aquatic-Plyo protocol. It yielded superior pain relief (p = 0.004, η2p = 0.14) and larger increases in quadriceps [120°/s (p = 0.006, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.008, η2p = 0.12)] and hamstring [120°/s (p = 0.007, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09)] peak torque. Moreover, the Aquatic-Plyo intervention drove greater reduction in functional disability (p = 0.03, η2p = 0.08) and notable enhancement in perceived health-related quality of life (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09).
CONCLUSION: Aquatic-Plyo exercises effectively reduces pain and disability while improving muscle strength and health-related quality of life in adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome, making it a valuable addition to conservative rehabilitation strategies.

title: The longitudinal relationship between physical capacity and self-perceived physical functioning after total hip and knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine longitudinal within-person effects between capacity and self-perceived performance during postoperative physiotherapy in patients with total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA/TKA).
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial on physiotherapy after THA and TKA using random intercept cross lagged panel models. Capacity was assessed with the 40-m fast-paced walk test (40 m FPWT) and the 30-s chair-stand test (30-s CST), and self-perceived performance with the Oxford Hip/Knee Score functioning subscale (OHS/OKS) and the Hip disability/Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical function Short form (HOOS-PS/KOOS-PS). Assessments were performed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: 312 THA (mean age 66, SD: 9; 53% female) and 312 TKA (mean age 67, SD: 8; 55% female) were included. From pre-surgery to 3 months, no effects were found between capacity and self-perceived performance in either THA or TKA.From 3 to 12 months, in THA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect (β 0.34, 95% CI 0.05-0.63) on HOOS-PS scores at 12 months. In TKA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect on both OKS functioning (β 0.24 95% CI 0.05-0.43) and KOOS-PS (β 0.29 95% CI 0.11-0.47) scores at 12 months. No other effects were observed.
CONCLUSION: From pre-surgery to 3 months, capacity and self-perceived performance showed no effects within individuals. However, during the early postoperative phase, gait speed may be a relevant treatment target to improve long-term self-perceived performance.

title: Efficacy of a Meta-Analysis-Recommended Immersion Protocol vs. Field-Practical Cold-Water Immersion Protocol for Performance Recovery: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
abstract: Kaji, R, Takeuchi, K, Okubo, S, and Yoshida, N. Efficacy of a meta-analysis-recommended immersion protocol vs. field-practical cold-water immersion protocol for performance recovery: A randomized crossover trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-We examined the effects of 2 cold-water immersion (CWI) protocols-15° C for 11 minutes and 10° C for 2.5 minutes-on performance recovery following exercise-induced fatigue. Fifteen male collegiate athletes completed 3 randomized crossover conditions with a 2-week washout: 15° C-11 minutes (evidence-based method), 10° C-2.5 minutes (field-practical method), and a seated-rest control. Outcomes included 20-m sprint time (T20), countermovement jump (CMJ), and Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 (YYIR2). The 20-m sprint time and CMJ were assessed before exercise (PreEx), immediately after exercise, immediately after the intervention, and at 1, 24, 48, and 72 hours postintervention, whereas YYIR2 was assessed at PreEx and at 72 hours postintervention. Physiological measures (tympanic temperature, skin temperatures, and heart rate) and perceptual measures (subjective fatigue and muscle soreness) were recorded. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The 10° C-2.5-minute protocol maintained T20 performance during the acute phase, whereas the 15° C-11-minute protocol facilitated later recovery. Countermovement jump performance transiently declined under both CWI conditions; however, a significant improvement at 72 hours occurred only with the 10° C-2.5-minute protocol. Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 performance did not differ between conditions. Thermal and cardiovascular responses varied by protocol and reflected recovery patterns. Subjective fatigue improved in both CWI conditions, whereas muscle soreness showed minimal differences. In conclusion, both evidence-based and field-practical CWI protocols enhanced recovery; however, they demonstrated distinct temporal profiles. The 10° C-2.5-minute protocol supported immediate restoration, whereas the 15° C-11-minute protocol promoted delayed recovery. For practical applications, protocol selection should align with sport-specific demands, recovery time, and performance objectives.

title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting.
METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed.
RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

title: The Potential Impact of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely prescribed for mood disorders. Their association with musculoskeletal side effects raises the question of potential SSRI impact on exercise-induced muscle damage and recovery.
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this prospective cohort study was to determine if SSRI use influences muscle function following a bout of eccentric exercise designed to induce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS).
METHODS: Subjects between 18 and 30 years of age were recruited in a university setting. This included 1 group taking SSRIs prescribed by their health care provider, and a control group not using SSRIs. Subjects performed a DOMS induction protocol consisting of 300 eccentric knee extensions on an isokinetic dynamometer. Muscle soreness, thigh circumference, quadriceps flexibility, and isometric quadriceps strength were measured at baseline and at 24-, 48-, 72-, and 96-hour post-DOMS protocol. Comparisons were made between SSRI users and control subjects.
RESULTS: Thirty-six subjects included 18 SSRI users and 18 controls. The DOMS protocol induced muscle soreness in both groups (P < .001 when compared with baseline). At 72 hours a between-group difference was observed for thigh muscle flexibility (MD = 11.2, SE = 5.0, 95% CI [0.9, 21.4], P = .033, ηp2 = .126) but no additional significant between-group differences in soreness, strength, thigh circumference, or flexibility were noted at any timepoint.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this population, SSRI use had no effect on muscle soreness, circumference, or strength of the quadriceps following eccentric DOMS-inducing exercise. A difference in flexibility between SSRI and control groups at a single time point likely reflects a Type 1 error and is not likely of clinical consequence. These findings suggest SSRIs do not impair short-term recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in healthy young adults, but potential SSRI impacts on longer-term training adaptations and recovery in athletic populations remain unknown.

title: Evolution of Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty: Two Decades of Evidence from the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Reverse shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) has evolved from a salvage procedure to a widely adopted reconstructive solution. This study performed a descriptive bibliometric and content-trend analysis of rTSA publications in the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery (JSES) from 2004-2025.
METHODS: A systematic review identified 506 clinical rTSA studies published in JSES between 2004 and 2025. Extracted variables included publication year, level of evidence, authorship, institution, geographic origin, research topic, demographics, indications, complications, and implant characteristics. Temporal trends were tested using Mann-Kendall trend test and segmented regression; the relationship between implant design representation and complication reporting was evaluated with Spearman rank correlation.
RESULTS: Annual publications increased significantly (BH-adjusted P < .001), peaking at 51 studies in 2023. Mean level of evidence improved (BH-adjusted P < .001), from 4.0 (2006) to 2.86 (2023). Early authorship centered on foundational surgeons (Frankle, Boileau, Walch) and European institutions, later diffusing globally. Mean age rose modestly, though this did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (BH-adjusted P = .077), stabilizing near 70-72 years after 2012. Research focus shifted from complications/technique toward outcomes after 2013, then toward instrumentation, rehabilitation, and cost. Osteoarthritis indications increased (BH-adjusted P = .005) while revision surgery declined (BH-adjusted P = .002). Implant design shifted from medialized to lateralized/non-Grammont configurations (both BH-adjusted P < .001). No individual complication subtype showed a significant temporal trend.
CONCLUSION: RTSA publication trends in JSES reflect the field's evolution from complication-focused study to evidence-driven refinement. Implant design, evidence level, and indications changed significantly, alongside, but not statistically linked to, complication reporting, informing future shoulder reconstruction research directions.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Literature Review, Bibliometric Analysis.

title: Training exposure, recovery, and injury incidence among course-based and competitive university Wushu Taolu practitioners: a 12-week prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether the large training-exposure difference between course-based and competitive-team university Wushu Taolu practitioners in China translates into a correspondingly different musculoskeletal health burden has not been well characterized prospectively.
METHODS: In this observational, non-randomized cohort study, 255 practitioners (128 course-based, 127 university-team; mean age 20.7 ± 1.5) were followed over four waves (T0-T3) across 12 weeks, with training load, sleep, recovery, health problems, and injury recorded using recall windows matched to each variable's time-scale.
RESULTS: University-team practitioners had substantially higher training exposure than course-based practitioners. The 12-week cumulative incidence of new injury was substantially higher in university-team practitioners than in course-based practitioners (68.9% vs. 20.0%; p < 0.001), with higher adjusted odds of injury (OR = 6.31, 95% CI 1.49-26.69). However, when injury occurrence was expressed relative to estimated training exposure, the between-group difference was much smaller: 10.56 versus 8.98 positive new-injury person-wave observations per 1,000 estimated training hours, respectively (IRR = 1.18, 95% CI 0.79-1.75). Prior injury within the preceding 12 months was strongly associated with subsequent injury (OR = 4.06, 95% CI 2.03-8.13).
CONCLUSION: University-team practitioners experienced a substantially greater absolute injury burden than course-based practitioners, whereas the between-group difference was much smaller when injury occurrence was expressed relative to estimated training exposure. Prior injury history was a strong marker of subsequent injury. Because group membership and training exposure were highly correlated and the study was observational, these findings should not be interpreted causally.

title: Effects of 30- and 90-Minute Afternoon Nap Opportunities on Field-Test Performance in Female Collegiate Basketball Players.
abstract: Afternoon napping is used as a recovery strategy in sport, but a scheduled nap opportunity is not equivalent to objectively verified sleep. This study compared no-nap seated wakefulness (N0), a 30-minute scheduled nap opportunity (N30), and a 90-minute scheduled nap opportunity (N90) in 18 female collegiate basketball players using a randomized, fully counterbalanced, three-period within-participant crossover design. Conditions were separated by at least 72 h and ended at 14:30, followed by a common 60 min wakefulness buffer, a standardized 15 min warm-up, and a fixed basketball field-test battery. Linear mixed-effects models included condition, period, and sequence as fixed effects, with participant as a random intercept; the nine omnibus condition tests were controlled for using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Four of nine outcomes remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction: the modified-505 first 10 m split, combined modified-505 completion time, three-quarter-court sprint time, and 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test final velocity. N90 differed from both N0 and N30 for these outcomes, whereas N30 did not differ from N0. The other five outcomes did not meet the false-discovery-rate threshold. Sensitivity analyses, including reanalysis of the pre-correction modified-505 data, preserved the same four-outcome pattern. Because sleep onset and duration were not objectively measured, the findings estimate the effects of assigned recovery-opportunity conditions rather than a physiological sleep-duration dose-response.

title: Determinants of Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychological and physical factors influence recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR). However, the relative contributions of psychological, subjective, and objective recovery measures to psychological readiness for return to sport remain unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To identify psychological, subjective, and objective recovery factors associated with psychological readiness to return to sport approximately 6 months after ACLR.
DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
SETTING: University laboratory.
PATIENTS OR OTHER PARTICIPANTS: A total of 58 participants (31 [53%] females; age = 18.95 ± 5.20 years), who completed standardized postoperative rehabilitation and follow-up testing at approximately 6 months after primary unilateral ACLR, were included.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: We measured psychological readiness using the ACL-Return to Sport after Injury (ACL-RSI) scale and conducted hierarchical regression analyses to examine predictors of psychological readiness across 4 conceptually ordered domains: (1) demographics (age, sex, and time since surgery), (2) generalized anxiety (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Anxiety Scale) and kinesiophobia (Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia 11), (3) knee-specific patient-reported outcomes (Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcomes Scale [KOOS] subscales of Pain, Symptoms, Quality of Life [QoL], and Sport), and (4) objective functional measures (quadriceps strength and single-legged hop symmetry). We conducted hierarchical linear regression in conceptually ordered blocks.
RESULTS: Demographic factors explained minimal variance in psychological readiness (1%-4%). Generalized anxiety contributed an additional 18.1%, and kinesiophobia (Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia 11, 22.3%), QoL (KOOS-QoL, 9.8%), and subjective sport function (KOOS-Sport, 5.3%) emerged as the strongest incremental predictors. Pain, symptoms, and objective function contributed little additional variance. The full model explained 70.5% of the variance in ACL-RSI scores (adjusted R 2 = 0.64, P < .001), and cross-validation produced a comparable R 2 (0.61), indicating good model generalizability and minimal overfitting.
CONCLUSIONS: Fear-related beliefs and perceived function exerted stronger influences on psychological readiness after ACLR than objective functional symmetry. These findings highlight the importance of biopsychosocial assessment models and sport-specific psychological measures to enhance return-to-sport decision-making and long-term recovery outcomes.

title: Excellent 2-Year Outcomes of MUIB All-Inside ACL Reconstruction: A Registry-Based Analysis of 63 Patients With Zero Graft Failure.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains a cornerstone of orthopedic sports medicine, yet graft failure rates are high despite advances in surgical techniques. The Modified UKM Internal Bracing (MUIB) technique combines all-inside ACLR with internal suture augmentation, potentially offering enhanced graft protection and improved outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study evaluated 63 patients who underwent isolated primary all-inside ACLR using the MUIB technique (19 allograft, 44 autograft) between 2020 and 2024. Outcome measures included International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores, graft failure rates, Single Leg Hop Test (SLHT) performance, and complication profiles at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: Both allograft and autograft groups demonstrated significant improvement from preoperative to 2-year follow-up (p < 0.001). There were no statistically significant differences observed between allograft and autograft groups across all outcome measures, suggesting that the MUIB technique may yield comparable outcomes regardless of graft type. Complete pain resolution (VAS 0) was achieved by 6 months in both groups. Notably, no graft re-tears were documented throughout the 2-year follow-up period, with 95.2% of patients achieving SLHT > 90% at 12 months. No infections, arthrofibrosis, or hardware-related complications requiring reoperation were recorded.
CONCLUSION: The MUIB all-inside ACLR technique yielded excellent 2-year outcomes in this cohort, characterized by a zero graft failure rate, complete pain resolution, and exceptional functional recovery. However, given the retrospective, uncontrolled design, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Prospective comparative studies are necessary to establish the efficacy and potential superiority of the MUIB technique relative to conventional ACLR approaches.

title: Urinary metabolomic signatures of muscle injury and recovery in elite football players.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Muscle injuries are a leading cause of time-loss in elite football, highlighting the need for objective biomarkers capable of reflecting the athlete's physiological state. Monitoring strategies rely predominantly on external load metrics and may not fully capture internal physiological responses to training and competition. Urinary metabolomics offers a non-invasive approach to characterize injury related physiological processes.
OBJECTIVES: To identify urinary metabolomic signatures associated with muscle injury in elite football players and to explore their potential utility for monitoring injury-related physiological stress and recovery.
METHODS: This observational longitudinal study included 287 urine samples collected from 121 elite male football players across two consecutive seasons. Samples were clinically classified as muscle injury (n = 30) or control (n = 257). Targeted UPLC-MS quantified amino acids and tryptophan-related metabolites. Univariate analysis, pathway over-representation analysis, and PLS-DA were applied to identify injury-associated metabolic patterns RESULTS: Muscle injury was associated with alterations in amino acid turnover, purine metabolism, energetic stress, and tryptophan catabolism. Exploratory pathway analysis suggested enrichment of amino acid-related pathways, although interpretation was limited by the targeted nature of the analytical panel. PLS-DA identified an injury-associated metabolic signature with a cross-validated AUROC of 0.88 (sensitivity 73%, specificity 88%; p < 0.003). Key discriminant metabolites included β-aminoisobutyric acid, hypoxanthine, xanthurenic acid, β-alanine, and alanine. Exploratory visual assessment of individual longitudinal trajectories suggested a return toward baseline during rehabilitation.
CONCLUSIONS: Urinary metabolomics identifies coordinated metabolic alterations associated with muscle injury in elite football players, supporting its potential as a future complementary tool to external load monitoring. Further validation in larger cohorts is required before these systemic signatures can be applied to clinical monitoring or recovery assessment.

title: Unsupervised Machine Learning Identifies Shared Biomechanical and Clinical Variation in Individuals with Knee Osteoarthritis and High BMI: A Secondary Analysis of the IDEA Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: High body mass index (BMI≥27 kg/m2) and aberrant gait biomechanics are primary risk factors for knee osteoarthritis (KOA), yet the specific loading patterns linked to clinical disease features remain unclear. Unsupervised machine learning (ML) was used to identify vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) waveform modes of variation and characterize the shared and individual variation between vGRF profiles and clinical features in individuals with KOA and high BMI.
METHODS: Baseline gait and clinical data from the Intensive Diet and Exercise for Arthritis (IDEA) trial (n=431; 29% male; 65±6 years; 34±4 kg/m2) were analyzed. vGRF waveforms (n=2,394) were represented using three functional data analysis methods: time- and bodyweight-normalization; elastic shape analysis; and optimal transport (OT). Principal component analysis extracted the dominant vGRF modes of variation, and Data Integration Via Analysis of Subspaces (DIVAS) quantified shared and individual variation among vGRF profiles and 40 clinical features.
RESULTS: A sustained loading phenotype emerged across all vGRF representations (lesser early and late stance vGRF; greater midstance vGRF). DIVAS identified shared variation between sustained loading and higher BMI, elevated inflammatory biomarkers, greater pain, worse KL grade, and slower walking speed. OT identified a temporal loading phenotype that shared variation with female sex.
CONCLUSIONS: Unsupervised ML identified a sustained loading biomechanical phenotype that shared variation with greater BMI, increased inflammation, worse radiographic severity, and slower walking speed. These data highlight the complex interplay among gait biomechanics and clinical KOA features in individuals with high BMI and may help to guide future work evaluating targeted gait retraining interventions.

title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

title: Consumer Grade Wearable Sensor Metrics Are Associated with Internal Forces at Common Running Injury Locations.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Inexpensive consumer-grade wearable sensors have expanded possibilities to assess, monitor, or modify a runner's gait. However, it is unclear which sensor-measured gait metrics are strongly associated with internal loading at common injury locations.
PURPOSE: To measure the association between gait metrics measured by consumer-grade wearable sensors and internal forces at the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint.
METHODS: 55 healthy runners wearing consumer-grade chest straps foot-pods completed a 38-minute run on an instrumented treadmill at 12 speeds from 70%-125% of self-reported typical running pace. A scaled musculoskeletal model derived from motion capture data and driven by static optimization was used to calculate Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint forces during stance for each speed. Functional regression models were used to estimate the associations of each of nine sensor-measured gait metrics with internal forces across stance, after adjusting for body mass and running speed.
RESULTS: At both the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint, cadence, vertical oscillation, and vertical ratio (vertical oscillation divided by step length) showed the strongest associations with internal forces (maximum of 0.4-0.6 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). Other wearable sensor-measured gait metrics, including stance time, leg stiffness, and stance time percent showed weaker associations (<0.4 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric).
CONCLUSIONS: Runners with higher-than-average cadence, vertical oscillation, or vertical ratio values experience marked differences in internal forces at the Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint. Of these gait metrics, cadence is the most practical for out-of-lab use because of its ease of accurate measurement with consumer-grade devices.

title: The relationship of grip and three-point pinch strength to ball velocity and elbow varus torque in high school pitchers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hand and forearm strength play an essential role in modulating and controlling forces across the elbow during pitching. In particular, grip and pinch strength reflect functional capacity of the flexor-pronator mass, which contributes to both performance and dynamic stability of the elbow. While diminished grip strength is often used clinically to monitor recovery following shoulder and elbow injury, values in adolescent pitchers are lacking. Furthermore, the relationship between grip and pinch strength with ball velocity and elbow varus torque remains poorly defined.
METHODS: Thirty-eight healthy high school pitchers (16.0 ± 0.9 years, 183.3 ± 6.0 cm, 78.1 ± 9.2 kg) were included in this study. Bilateral grip and three-point pinch strength were assessed prior to pitching. Pitchers were then analyzed using 3D motion capture (480 Hz) and ball velocity was recorded with Trackman throwing fastballs. The pitch with the greatest ball velocity was used in the analysis. Paired t-tests compared dominant and non-dominant grip and pinch strength, and linear regression examined relationships between strength, ball velocity, and elbow torque (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Dominant arm grip strength was greater than the non-dominant throwing arm (P = .001), while pinch strength showed no side to side differences (P = .696). Dominant grip strength demonstrated weak associations with height (r2 = 0.221, P = .002), weight (r2 = 0.217, P = .002), and ball velocity (r2 = 0.116, P = .021). No significant relationships were found between grip strength and elbow varus torque. Pinch strength was not associated with height, weight, age, elbow varus torque, or ball velocity.
DISCUSSION: While forearm musculature is thought to enhance medial elbow stability, grip and pinch strength were not associated with elbow varus torque in high school pitchers. These results suggest that static hand strength measures may not reflect the complex, dynamic demands placed on the elbow during pitching. Further evaluation may be necessary to determine secondary impact such as load and subsequent fatigue on the flexor pronator complex.
CONCLUSION: Grip and pinch strength values in high school pitchers may serve as reference data for clinicians assessing adolescent pitchers. Grip strength demonstrated a weak association with ball velocity; however, neither grip nor pinch strength was significantly related to elbow loading. This highlights the need for future work examining dynamic forearm muscle function in injury risk, recovery, and performance.

title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases.
METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047).
CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Structured Physiotherapy Improves Functional Outcomes in Acromegalic Arthropathy After Biochemical Remission: A Prospective Controlled Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Musculoskeletal symptoms frequently persist in acromegaly despite biochemical remission, yet the impact of structured physiotherapy on pain, stiffness, and function remains poorly defined.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a standardized knee-focused physiotherapy program in controlled acromegaly and to identify clinical predictors of treatment responsiveness.
METHODS: Thirteen patients with acromegaly in remission and 13 age-, gender-, and BMI-matched individuals with primary knee osteoarthritis completed a 15-session physiotherapy program. Outcomes were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) and WOMAC. Minimal clinically significant difference (MCID) thresholds (≥2 for BPI, ≥10 for WOMAC) determined meaningful improvement. Correlation analyses examined associations between clinical variables and Δ scores.
RESULTS: Acromegaly patients showed significant improvements in all BPI and WOMAC domains (p<0.001). MCID was achieved by 85% for BPI and 100% for WOMAC Total. Pain and function improved most, whereas stiffness showed limited responsiveness. Compared with osteoarthritis controls, acromegaly patients demonstrated smaller Δ changes; baseline-adjusted analyses (ANCOVA) indicated that this attenuated response was largely explained by greater baseline severity in the control group, whereas the persistently greater stiffness in acromegaly remained significant even after adjustment. BMI correlated positively with improvements in BPI Total (r = 0.63) and BPI Pain Severity (r = 0.69), while adenoma size correlated negatively with both measures (r = -0.57 and -0.60). BMI showed a negative association with WOMAC Total improvement (r = -0.59). Stiffness changes were strongly negatively correlated with pretreatment IGF-1 (r = -0.77).
CONCLUSION: Structured physiotherapy yields clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function in acromegaly, while stiffness appears less reversible and more structurally driven. Early musculoskeletal assessment and physiotherapy integration may enhance long-term management.

title: Sleep-related metrics that predict training intensity: an exploratory study in women's college athletics.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In recent years, the development of wearable monitoring technologies has expanded objective assessments of workload and fatigue, predominantly via heart rate (HR)-based markers (e.g., heart rate variability, resting heart rate). There are also perception-based markers of exertion commonly used in high-performance training settings, such as rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scales. Previous research has shown that these markers do not measure identical but rather complementary aspects of exertion, but limited data exist on the relationships between objective and subjective markers at the daily level; data which may be especially important for understanding how to best monitor for effort or overtraining. This study will characterize both HR- and perception-based markers of exertion at the daily level in women's college athletes. Additionally, given the powerful influence of sleep on both athletic performance and perceptions of physical exertion, we further explored how sleep behaviors at the within- and between-person level relate to daily assessments of subjective and objective exertion.
METHODS: Thirteen women's college athletes continuously wore a WHOOP activity monitor for this two-week observational study. RPE was self-reported within 30 min of completing a training session or competition and prior to viewing WHOOP data.
RESULTS: A series of descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation were conducted to describe the relationship between RPE and activity strain on a daily level among the population studied. A series of linear mixed-effects models demonstrated worse sleep on average (i.e., more debt, poorer sleep performance) was associated with higher HR-based markers of exertion; however, within-person elevations in sleep consistency, but more sleep need on average was associated with higher HR-based measures of exertion and lower perceptions of exertion.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings support the need for additional research to better understand the drivers of daily markers of exertion to enhance the health and performance of athletes.

title: Technical evaluation of transport-derived movement trajectories during knee osteoarthritis rehabilitation.
abstract: Wearable inertial sensors enable repeated movement recording during knee osteoarthritis rehabilitation, but methods for summarizing multivariable changes across routine sessions remain exploratory. This retrospective technical evaluation examined a normalized transport-derived deviation (NTD) constructed from paired shank-mounted inertial measurement units. Seven participants contributed 46 paired-sensor sessions over 45 d. An approximately 30 s active movement segment from each session was divided into 13 windows and represented using 58 time-domain, frequency-domain and cross-sensor features. Session distributions were compared with each participant's first usable sensor session using an archived entropically regularized transport implementation. The output was normalized by the baseline-to-final-session value. Mean NTD values at the scheduled assessment days were 0.00, 0.02, 0.23, 0.63 and 1.00. 14 of the 46 displayed values were structurally constrained baseline or final values; no monotonic constraint was applied to the 32 interior observations, which formed non-decreasing trajectories. At interior scheduled days 5, 15 and 30, absolute differences between mean NTD and participant-adjusted normalized elapsed time were 0.057, 0.076 and 0.019. 21 of the 46 archived calculations reached the 500-iteration limit without meeting the 1 × 10-6residual criterion. A log-domain stabilized recomputation of all 46 primary comparisons satisfied a 1 × 10-8criterion, with a mean absolute archived-to-stabilized NTD difference of 0.004 (maximum 0.018) across the 32 interior observations. Across support-point counts of 100-1000, interior archived NTD values changed by 0.009-0.026 on average. Routine paired-shank recordings were organized into ordered longitudinal trajectories and the resulting trajectory structure was numerically reproducible under the evaluated implementation. NTD should presently be interpreted as an implementation-specific retrospective coordinate rather than a validated rehabilitation outcome. By defining the requirements for standardized movement tasks, prospective normalization and reproducible sensor placement, these findings provide a practical foundation for prospective validation of transport-based rehabilitation assessment.

title: Effect of Adjunctive Mifepristone Pre-treatment on Operative Efficiency and Postoperative Recovery in Cesarean Scar Pregnancy Undergoing Curettage After Uterine Artery Embolization.
abstract:
AIM: This study aims to evaluate whether short-course mifepristone pre-treatment improves procedural efficiency and early recovery after uterine artery embolization (UAE), followed by dilation and curettage (D&C) for cesarean scar pregnancy.
METHODS: This retrospective study recruited 108 patients with cesarean scar pregnancy who underwent dilation and D&C between January 2020 and July 2023. Patients were divided into 2 groups according to the pre-treatment approach. The control group (n = 65) received pre-treatment with UAE alone, while the study group (n = 43) received pre-treatment with mifepristone in addition to the treatment used in the control group. The two groups were compared for operative metrics, early recovery, and postoperative adverse events. Serum β-human chorionic gonadotrophin (β-hCG) levels were evaluated upon admission and again on postoperative day 1. Patients were followed for one year to assess pregnancy-related outcomes, and the findings were compared between the two groups.
RESULTS: In the study group, the surgery duration was shorter, and the intraoperative blood loss was lower than in the control group (p < 0.05). The length of hospital stay was comparable between the two groups (p > 0.05). Similarly, the incidences of repeat D&C, massive hemorrhage, and re-embolization of the uterine artery were also comparable between groups (p > 0.05). There were no cases of conversion to laparotomy or hysterectomy in either group. At the time of admission, the β-hCG levels in the study group were not significantly different from those in the control group. However, on the first day after the procedure, the β-hCG levels in the study group were lower than those in the control group, but the difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.051). The study group had a shorter duration of vaginal bleeding and achieved normal menstrual function earlier than the control group (p < 0.05). The menstrual cycle was comparable between the two groups (p > 0.05). The incidences of fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, abnormal liver function, and intrauterine adhesions were also comparable between the two groups (p > 0.05). Follow-up analysis showed no significant differences between the two groups in subsequent pregnancy or recurrence of cesarean scar pregnancy (p > 0.05). Time to pregnancy was descriptively reported only among patients who achieved pregnancy and was not statistically compared because of the small number of events.
CONCLUSIONS: Incorporating short-course mifepristone pre-treatment to a standard uterine artery embolization-D&C strategy for cesarean scar pregnancy was associated with shorter operative time and better early recovery profiles, with satisfactory safety outcomes.

title: Talking about menstruation in professional women's sport: gendered communication between athletes, coaches and team-mates.
abstract: Communication about menstruation remains uneven within sporting environments despite growing recognition of the importance of menstrual health for athletes. This article investigates how female athletes communicate about menstruation and how gendered hierarchies shape these interactions. The analysis is based on responses to an online questionnaire completed by Polish professional athletes (N = 253). The findings indicate that menstruation is seldom discussed between athletes and coaches, with participants identifying social and institutional barriers, including menstrual taboo and the predominance of male coaches. In contrast, athletes reported discussing menstruation more openly with female team-mates, where such conversations often facilitated mutual support and the sharing of experiential knowledge about menstrual health. These interactions suggest that women's teams can function as 'counterspaces' where menstrual experiences can be acknowledged and normalised in ways largely absent from coach-athlete relationships. Findings highlight the importance of creating environments in which menstrual health can be openly discussed, as limited communication about menstruation may restrict athletes' access to information, support, and health-related guidance. By examining menstruation as a topic of health-related communication, the study contributes to scholarship on gender, embodiment and menstrual health, highlighting how institutional hierarchies shape the visibility and discussion of bodily processes across different social contexts.

title: Cross-sectional associations of maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors with athlete engagement among provincial- and municipal-level athletes in Sichuan, China.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors are potentially modifiable daily practices, yet their relationship with the psychological state that sustains sport involvement remains unclear. This study examined cross-sectional associations among maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors (MSHB), multidimensional fatigue, difficulties in emotion regulation, and athlete engagement, including three model-based indirect associations.
METHODS: A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was completed by 317 adult athletes recruited from provincial- and municipal-level teams in Sichuan Province, China. Participants represented table tennis, badminton, tennis, basketball, volleyball, and football. The Sleep Hygiene Index, the Chinese Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory, the DERS-16, and the Athlete Engagement Questionnaire were administered. A reflective partial least squares structural equation model was estimated with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Measurement quality, construct differentiation, common-method diagnostics, out-of-sample prediction, demographic adjustment, alternative cross-sectional specifications, and subgroup robustness were evaluated.
RESULTS: More frequent MSHB were associated with greater fatigue [β = 0.491, 95% CI (0.408, 0.573)], greater difficulties in emotion regulation [β = 0.178, 95% CI (0.079, 0.274)], and lower athlete engagement [β = -0.264, 95% CI (-0.370, -0.161)]. Fatigue was associated with greater difficulties in emotion regulation [β = 0.588, 95% CI (0.500, 0.673)] and lower engagement [β = -0.325, 95% CI (-0.446, -0.205)]; difficulties in emotion regulation were also associated with lower engagement [β = -0.232, 95% CI (-0.351, -0.108)]. The total indirect association was [β = -0.268, 95% CI (-0.338, -0.204)], and the model explained 47.2% of engagement variance. Demographic adjustment yielded comparable estimates. Reverse-order and parallel specifications fitted the cross-sectional covariance structure equally well.
CONCLUSION: Within the sampled setting, more frequent MSHB co-occurred with greater fatigue, more difficulties in emotion regulation, and lower athlete engagement. Fatigue accounted for the largest specific indirect association. The single-occasion self-report design leaves actual sleep disturbance, temporal sequence, and causal effects unresolved.

title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR).
METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction.
RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR.
CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

title: The Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer: proposal for an ultrasound-based muscle injury classification.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To propose a novel ultrasound-based classification system for muscle injuries in soccer players, termed the Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer (SOMICS), and to evaluate its association, ordinal consistency, and agreement with the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a cross-sectional observational study including 51 adolescent male soccer players (11-19 years of age) with suspected acute myotendinous injuries. All athletes underwent ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 h after injury. Four experienced radiologists, working independently, reviewed the images.
RESULTS: Interobserver agreement was substantial for ultrasound (κ = 0.65) and MRI (κ = 0.70). A strong ordinal correlation was observed between SOMICS and BAMIC categories (ρ = 0.80; p < 0.001), with a statistically significant association (χ2 = 52.53; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The SOMICS demonstrated significant association, ordinal consistency, and substantial agreement with the BAMIC for severity stratification of muscle injuries. Although not intended to replace MRI-based classifications for prognostic decision-making, the SOMICS provides a structured, reproducible ultrasound-based approach that may be useful in clinical settings where MRI is not readily available or as a first-line imaging tool.

title: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium in adolescent athletes with acute groin pain: clinical and MRI features of a radiograph-occult injury pattern.
abstract: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is an uncommon MRI finding in young athletes with acute groin pain and is frequently occult on plain radiographs. This study aimed to characterize its clinical presentation, MRI findings, associated injuries, and return-to-sport outcomes. This retrospective single-center case series included athletes aged ≤22 years who underwent MRI for acute sports-related groin pain with negative or inconclusive radiographs between 2017 and 2025. Patients meeting predefined MRI criteria for subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium were identified, and clinical, imaging, and outcome data were analyzed descriptively. Twenty of 91 patients (22.0%) met the MRI criteria. Their mean age was 13.9 ± 1.5 years, 19 (95%) were male, and 18 (90%) had open physes. Periosteal elevation was present in all patients, and 19 (95%) demonstrated a predominantly subperiosteal fluid collection, most commonly with a lentiform configuration. Associated anterior inferior iliac spine avulsion injury or intramuscular iliacus injury was identified in 10 patients (50%). All patients were managed nonoperatively and returned to unrestricted sports participation after progressive rehabilitation at a mean of 4.5 ± 2.2 weeks. Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is a reproducible MRI finding in predominantly skeletally immature athletes with acute sports-related groin pain and negative or inconclusive radiographs. Recognition of periosteal elevation with a predominantly subperiosteal fluid collection may facilitate diagnosis of this radiograph-occult injury pattern. Although the underlying injury mechanism remains hypothetical, prospective studies are needed to clarify its clinical significance.

title: Biomechanical comparison of an ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler construct and an open Krackow construct for Achilles tendon repair: a cadaver study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Open Achilles tendon repair can cause wound-related complications. Ultrasound-guided minimally invasive repair may reduce soft-tissue disruption, but its biomechanical performance requires further evaluation. This study compared the initial biomechanical performance of an ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler construct with an open Krackow construct in a cadaveric model.
METHODS: Twelve fresh-frozen cadaveric Achilles tendons were transected 4 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion and allocated to an open Krackow group (n = 6) or an ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler group (n = 6). Testing included 10 loading cycles (50 N at 2.1 mm/s) followed by pull-to-failure testing (25 mm/s). Maximum load to failure and failure modes were recorded.
FINDINGS: No statistically significant difference in maximum load to failure was observed between the Krackow (149.2 ± 39.0 N) and ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler (148.5 ± 22.8 N) constructs (Mann-Whitney U test, U = 18, p > 0.05). All specimens completed the initial cyclic loading phase. In the minimally invasive group, three specimens failed after 5-mm gapping and three by suture knot breakage; in the Krackow group, five failed after 5-mm gapping and one by suture rupture.
INTERPRETATION: The ultrasound-guided minimally invasive modified Kessler construct demonstrated load-to-failure performance comparable to the open Krackow construct. When both repairs use four core strands crossing the repair site, the overall construct may reduce the mechanical difference expected from suture configuration alone. However, this small cadaveric cohort does not establish formal biomechanical equivalence or isolate the independent contribution of ultrasound guidance.

title: The Hidden Cost: Effects of Prior Coordinative, Sprint, and Combined Tasks on Physical Performance During Small-Sided Games in Youth Soccer Players.
abstract: This study compared the effects of sprint (SPRT), coordinative (COORD), and combined (COMB) exercises on physical performance in small-sided games (SSGs). Twenty-four under-16 male soccer players participated in a repeated-measures design, performing four interventions (Control [CONT], SPRT, COORD, and COMB) prior to SSGs in a 4v4+GK format. The total distance, distance covered in different speed zones, acceleration, and deceleration were analyzed. Data were assessed using generalized estimating equations, adopting p ≤ .05 for statistical significance. A lower total distance (p = .02) and shorter distances in the initial acceleration zones (0.0-0.99 m·s-2; p = .013) were observed after COMB compared with CONT. A similar result was also observed in the deceleration zone between -2.00 and -2.99 m·s-2, where a lower value was found after COMB compared to CONT (p = .043). Furthermore, COMB (p = .021) and SPRT (p = .023) reduced the number of decelerations compared with CONT. Overall, the combined condition was associated with selective reductions in specific physical performance variables during subsequent SSGs, whereas most speed-zone, acceleration, and deceleration variables remained unchanged. Therefore, combined coordinative and sprint tasks should be incorporated with caution when SSGs are intended to provide a high physical stimulus.

title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise.
abstract: The duration of the repeated-bout effect following eccentric knee-extensor exercise remains undefined, despite its widespread use in muscle damage research and training. The present study examined how long this protective effect persists in the knee extensors. Forty-eight young men performed two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 × 15 repetitions at 60°/s). Four independent groups performed the second bout 3, 6, 9, or 12 weeks after the first. Isometric torque, range of motion (ROM), delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), muscle thickness, echo intensity, creatine kinase (CK), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) were assessed before and 2 and 4 days after each bout. Baseline-adjusted linear mixed-effects models were used to compare responses between bouts, complemented by equivalence testing at 12 weeks. The repeated-bout effect was evident at 3 and 6 weeks across most outcomes and remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers. At 12 weeks, no significant differences between bouts were observed at either day 2 or day 4 for any outcome. Exploratory equivalence analyses further indicated that the effect was no longer meaningfully present at these time points for isometric torque, ROM, DOMS, muscle thickness, and echo intensity, whereas the findings for CK and hs-CRP remained inconclusive. Overall, the repeated-bout effect may persist for some outcomes for up to 9 weeks, whereas by 12 weeks no meaningful effect was detectable at the assessed post-exercise time points. This time course can guide the design of muscle damage studies and the scheduling of eccentric training sessions.

title: Association Between Hormone Variability and Anaerobic Performance in Recreationally Active Women: An Exploratory Study Using Mixed-Effect Location Scale Models.
abstract: Ramey, KT, Unrein, CL, Yang, C-H, and Hirsch, KR. Association between hormone variability and anaerobic performance in recreationally active women: An exploratory study using mixed-effect location scale models. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study explored the application of mixed-effects location scale modeling (MELS) to examine how daily variability in urinary estrogen (E), progesterone (PdG), and their ratio (E:P) relates to repeated sprint performance (peak power [PP], average power [AP], power drop [PD], and fatigue index [FI]) across low and high hormone phases in healthy, recreationally active eumenorrheic (n = 8) women and hormonal contraceptive users (intrauterine device = 6; oral contraception = 10; age: 24.7 ± 4.2 years; height: 165.5 ± 6.5 cm; body mass: 63.0 ± 6.7 kg). Subjects completed 30.4 ± 10.7 days of at-home urine hormone testing for E (ng⋅ml-1), PdG (µg⋅ml-1), and calculate E:P ratio. A repeated sprint test (10 × [6 seconds sprint: 30 seconds rest]) on a cycle ergometer was completed during both the low and high hormone phases to evaluate sprint performance. Fatigue index (%) was recorded, and PP (W), AP (W), and PD (W) were averaged across sprints. Associations between E, P, and E:P with FI, PP, AP, and PD were examined using separate MELS models. Paired t-tests assessed phase differences, and Pearson correlations evaluated relationships between day-of-testing hormone levels and performance. Day-of-testing E (p < 0.001), PdG (p < 0.001), PP (p = 0.047), and AP (p = 0.016) were significantly higher in the high hormone phase, and PdG correlated positively with PD (r = 0.574, p = 0.003). Greater individual E variability was associated with lower PP (Low: Estimate = -48.47, p = 0.004; High: Estimate = -50.18, p = 0.009) and AP (Low: Estimate = -46.75, p = 0.005; High: Estimate = -42.04, p = 0.024), remaining significant after controlling for percent body fat and lean mass (p = 0.008-0.022). These findings suggest hormonal instability may meaningfully influence anaerobic performance. This study introduces novel methodology and statistical framework that captures dynamic hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle and can be used to evaluate hormonal influence on female physiology and performance variability.

title: Non-Surgical Therapies for Knee Osteoarthritis: Current Evidence and Emerging Strategies.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by pain, stiffness, and functional impairment. As many patients seek to avoid surgery, a synthesis of conservative treatment options is clinically relevant for evidence-based management.
METHODS: A structured PubMed literature search was conducted through December 15, 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, cohort and case-control studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses evaluating nonsurgical interventions for knee OA. Extracted outcomes included pain, function, safety, and comparative effectiveness across reported follow-up durations.
RESULTS: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid (HA) has a favorable safety profile and may delay progression to total knee arthroplasty, though benefits over placebo are modest and guideline recommendations inconsistent. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) improves pain and function and may outperform HA, although outcomes vary with preparation methods and study quality. Autologous conditioned serum and dextrose prolotherapy demonstrate symptomatic benefit, whereas corticosteroid injections primarily provide short-term relief. Disease-modifying osteoarthritis drugs (DMOADs), including sprifermin, lorecivivint, LNA043, cathepsin-K inhibition, ADAMTS-5 inhibition, and repurposed metabolic agents such as metformin, are emerging investigational strategies with variable structural and symptomatic results. Early evidence suggests mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies may improve outcomes but remain investigational. Core conservative measures, including exercise therapy, physical therapy, and weight reduction, consistently reduce pain and improve function. Assistive devices and valgus bracing provide additional symptomatic and biomechanical benefit. Among device-based interventions, cooled radiofrequency ablation offers durable pain relief compared with HA or corticosteroids, while sustained acoustic medicine and extracorporeal shockwave therapy show functional improvement; evidence for pulsed electromagnetic field therapy is mixed. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs provide effective analgesia with reduced systemic risk.
CONCLUSION: Non-surgical management of knee OA should follow a stepwise approach, with rehabilitation and weight optimization as first-line therapy, selective injection- and device-based options for persistent symptoms, and timely surgical referral when disability remains refractory. Future progress will depend on standardized protocols and higher-quality long-term comparative trials to improve treatment selection and disease modification.

title: Editorial Commentary: Measuring Surgical Success in Athletes Requires More Than Generic Scores: It Is Time to Prioritize Athlete-Specific Outcomes.
abstract: Shoulder instability disproportionately affects young contact and collision athletes, for whom successful treatment requires more than the restoration of basic shoulder function. Recent systematic review reveals that conventional patient-reported outcomes dominated outcome reporting, whereas fewer than half of studies reported return to sport and only 15% included objective sport-specific performance measures. Common scores such as American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons, Rowe, and Western Ontario Shoulder Instability inadequately capture return to preinjury level, athletic performance, and durability of return to sport. Outcomes in athletes should therefore combine sport-specific patient-reported outcomes, clearly defined return to sport, and objective performance measures. Artificial intelligence may further improve assessment by dynamically tailoring follow-up to an athlete's sport and position. Traditional shoulder scores may tell us how well the shoulder functions, but they are not enough to tell us how well the athlete performs.

title: Gait Retraining for Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome: A Biomechanical Approach to Pain Relief and Performance Optimization.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is common among runners and is linked to biomechanical dysfunctions that increase patellofemoral joint stress. Gait retraining has been proposed to redistribute this loading, but the effectiveness of different retraining strategies and their long-term impact remain unclear. This scoping review synthesizes existing evidence on gait retraining strategies for PFPS, focusing on pain, function, and biomechanics.
DATA SOURCES: MEDLINE, Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus, PEDro, and Web of Science were searched, following the methodological framework of the Joanna Briggs Institute for scoping reviews. Studies investigating gait retraining interventions in runners diagnosed with PFPS were included. Key outcomes were pain reduction, functional improvement, biomechanical adaptations, and adverse effects.
MAIN RESULTS: Three randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria, examining cadence modification, impact reduction, and foot strike adjustments. Intervention groups experienced significant pain reduction, with Visual Analog Scale scores improving by 2 to 4 points, alongside functional gains reflected by increased Kujala and Knee Outcome Survey of the Activities of Daily Living Scale scores. Biomechanical adaptations included decreased patellofemoral joint stress, lower impact forces, and improved load distribution. Some participants reported transient calf discomfort during the adaptation period, which resolved over time.
CONCLUSIONS: Gait retraining is an effective intervention for runners with PFPS, showing sustained pain relief, functional improvement, and biomechanical benefits. Individualized protocols and gradual implementation are essential to optimize outcomes and minimize discomfort. Future research should address long-term retention of gait modifications, optimal training parameters, and applicability beyond runners.

title: Additive effects of active vitamin D3 or vitamin E administration on therapeutic lower-limb home exercise for knee osteoarthritis: A pilot prospective randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quadriceps weakness, inflammation, and reduced physical function are common in knee osteoarthritis (OA), and lower limb exercise therapy is an established non-pharmacological treatment. Vitamin D3 (vit D3) and vitamin E (vit E) have been proposed as adjunctive therapies; however, clinical findings are inconsistent. We aimed to examine whether combining lower limb home exercises with oral active vit D3 or vit E supplementation provides additive benefits compared with home exercise alone in women with symptomatic knee OA.
METHODS: Eighty-eight postmenopausal women with knee OA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-4; 71.9 ± 5.6 years) were randomly assigned to receive therapeutic lower limb home exercise only, home exercise with active vit D3 administration, or home exercise with vit E administration. Participants performed isometric lower limb exercises twice daily for 24 weeks. Subsequently, they were assessed using the Japanese knee osteoarthritis measure (JKOM) as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were short-form health survey, grip strength, quadriceps muscle strength, 10-m walk test, inflammatory markers, bone mineral density, and body composition. For data analyses, we used paired and independent t tests, analysis of variance, and analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, body mass index, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade.
RESULTS: Eighty participants completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements in JKOM score, quadriceps muscle strength, and 10-m walk test. Grip strength improved significantly only in the group that received active vit D. No significant between-group differences were observed in JKOM scores, short-form health survey-36, muscle strength, or physical performance. Inflammatory markers decreased significantly in the vit E group, although between-group differences were not observed. No other significant between-group differences were found, except in bone mineral density.
CONCLUSIONS: Administering active vit D3 or vit E for 24 weeks as an adjunct to lower limb home exercises did not yield significant additive effects on symptoms, muscle strength, or physical performance in women with knee OA. Exercise therapy alone remained effective, and vitamin supplementation showed nutrient-specific trends.

title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation and Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation in Athletes: Optimizing Athletic Performance and Sleep Quality Through Neuromodulation.
abstract: Neuromodulation is a procedure relying on the delivery of specific stimuli to selected sites of the nervous system and hereby influencing its activity. Even though the underlying neurobiological mechanisms are not yet fully elucidated and the research is still ongoing, neuromodulation is already being used as an intervention for various mental conditions and insomnia, or it may even improve the physical performance of athletes. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the effects of specific neuromodulation techniques on performance and sleep quality in athletes, focusing on cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). PubMed, SCOPUS, Web of Science and Ovid MEDLINE databases were searched for relevant articles. All types of publications were taken into account, but original studies, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and meta-analyses were given priority. Current evidence shows that while tDCS may improve athletic performance, especially endurance and sport-specific skills, its impact on sleep in athletes is inconclusive. This method may increase subjectively reported total sleep time and subjective sleep quality, but no objective improvement has been demonstrated. CES findings are preliminary: evidence from the small trials suggests improvement of selected objective sleep parameters, but the evidence base is limited to two small studies, one of which lacked a sham condition. In conclusion, non-invasive neuromodulation methods, specifically tDCS and CES, may impact athletic performance and help treat sleep disorders in athletes. Neuromodulation should not be viewed as a standalone method, but rather a complementary tool to other known interventions for insomnia in athletes. Although the aforementioned techniques show promising results, the research on this topic is limited and requires further evaluation.

title: Effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate on exercise-induced biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation in federated road cyclists.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined the effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate (CPH) on biomarkers associated with exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation in federated male road cyclists.
METHODS: Twenty-four participants completed a 14-day intervention receiving either 12 g/day of chickpea protein hydrolysate (EXP) or a placebo (PLA) following training sessions. The selected dose was based on previous studies demonstrating antioxidant and immunomodulatory bioactive properties of the hydrolysate. Nutritional intake and training were registered. Body composition and biochemical markers of muscle damage and inflammation were assessed before and after the study.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in body composition, training load, or dietary intake between groups, indicating controlled experimental conditions. However, between-group analyses of change scores revealed significant differences for lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; p = 0.04) and C-reactive protein (CRP; p = 0.02), favoring the experimental group. LDH decreased in the EXP group while increasing slightly in the placebo group, whereas CRP decreased in EXP and increased in PLA. Although creatine kinase (CK) showed a favorable pattern in the EXP group, the between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.062). Myoglobin followed a similar downward trend. The high baseline protein intake (>2 g/kg/day) and short intervention duration may have limited changes in body composition, nevertheless, the observed biomarker responses suggest that CPH supplementation may influence selected physiological processes associated with exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress.
CONCLUSIONS: In trained cyclists with high habitual protein intakes, 14 days of CPH supplementation did not alter body composition but was associated with favorable changes in selected biomarkers related to exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress compared with placebo. Given the short intervention period and the absence of direct assessments of recovery or performance, these findings should be interpreted as short-term biochemical responses. Further studies are required to determine their physiological relevance and whether these biomarker changes translate into meaningful improvements in recovery, training adaptation, or athletic performance.

title: Evaluation, Management, and Return-To-Sport Guidelines for Cervical Spine Injuries in Athletes: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Study DesignNarrative review.ObjectivesTo synthesize current evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, classification, evaluation, and imaging of cervical spine injuries (CSI) in athletes and propose a practical framework for return-to-sport (RTS) decision-making.MethodsA review of the most recent and relevant published studies and consensus statements was performed, focusing on athletic cervical spine pathology. Key domains included on-field assessment, imaging modalities, clinical clearance criteria, and sport-specific risk considerations. All literature published in reputable journals, preferably available through well-regarded databases such as Scopus and PubMed, was eligible for inclusion, with preference given to the most recent publications related to any given topic.ResultsThe reviewed literature supports that RTS across CSI types requires resolution of symptoms, normal neurologic examination, restoration of painless cervical range of motion and strength, and radiographic evidence of healing or stability. MRI is consistently recommended for identifying high-risk features such as canal stenosis, cord signal change, or ligamentous disruption. Sport-specific risk stratification is supported by data showing higher reinjury rates in collision sports. Evidence remains heterogeneous, with substantial variation in specialist recommendations.ConclusionsSafe RTS after CSI requires comprehensive clinical and imaging assessment, recognition of sport-specific risks, and shared decision-making to prioritize athlete safety while avoiding unnecessary restrictions.
