title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol.
METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength.
RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status.
CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

title: Programmable 4D printing of sustainable multifunctional photoresins with tissue-matched mechanics for interfacial tissue regeneration.
abstract: The integrative regeneration of articular cartilage and subchondral bone remains a major clinical challenge due to the difficulties of mimicking the spatial and compositional complexity of native osteochondral tissues in artificial implants. To overcome these limitations, 3D printing has enabled personalized solutions, going beyond traditional plug-shaped scaffolds that are limited to repairing small, cylindrical focal defects. In this study, we report solvent-free 4D printing of olive oil-derived fatty amide-based acrylate photoresin for osteochondral tissue engineering applications. The physicochemical properties of the printed polymers were fine-tuned using acrylic acid as a comonomer. With optimized printing conditions, the resin can be printed into high-resolution objects with each layer of ∼50-100 μm. Depending on the resin composition, the mechanical properties of the printed polymers vary between ∼200-1400 kPa with ∼210-420% strain under tensile setting, and ∼26-98 MPa at ∼80% strain under compressive setting. The mechanical properties of the printed polymers are comparable to those of various interfacial soft tissues, including ligaments, articular cartilage, and soft collagenous bone, indicating their potential for interfacial tissue engineering applications. Furthermore, the printed polymers showed near-body temperature-responsive shape memory (4D) properties with a recovery ratio of ∼99% for optimized resin composition. In addition, the printed polymers exhibited excellent bactericidal antimicrobial activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, highlighting their multifunctional nature. More importantly, the printed polymers exhibited good cytocompatibility (cell viability ∼≥90% across all samples compared to control) toward adipose-derived human mesenchymal stem cells, facilitating growth factor-free osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation, which confirms their potential for osteochondral tissue regeneration. Overall, the newly developed biobased resin offers a low-cost, sustainable alternative for 4D printing of personalized implants for osteochondral tissue regeneration.

title: UEFA consensus guidelines on anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in Women's football - part one: risk factors and prevention.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are among the most burdensome injuries in women's football, carrying significant consequences for players and the football community. To develop practical, evidence-based guidelines for ACL injury prevention, UEFA convened a multidisciplinary expert panel of 31 doctors, sports scientists, physiotherapists, and a player. Using the RAND-UCLA Appropriateness Method, 101 evidence statements were synthesised from existing literature and subjected to a modified Delphi process with three rounds of confidential voting. Consensus was reached on 88 statements. Through online and in-person discussions, this evidence was integrated with expert and clinical and practical judgement to produce actionable recommendations tailored to women's football. The guidelines conclude that ACL injuries in women's football typically occur in non-contact situations during high-intensity movements such as cutting, pressing, or landing, and may be influenced by a combination of modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Proposed modifiable factors include deficits in neuromuscular control, strength, and movement quality, which can be addressed through multicomponent prevention strategies. These programmes were identified as the most effective, incorporating plyometric, strength, and proximal control exercises performed two to three times per week for 15 to 20 minutes, with evidence showing they can reduce non-contact ACL injuries when adherence is high. Successful implementation requires context-specific tailoring, embedding programmes into routine training, and addressing barriers such as limited resources, time constraints, and lack of coach education. The guidelines recommend enhancing buy-in through co-creation with coaches and players, integrating prevention into existing practice, and strengthening organisational and policy support to sustain long-term adoption.

title: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation.
METHODS: This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening.
RESULTS: Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

title: Summary of the 2026 Professionals in Nutrition for Exercise and Sport "10 Questions/10 Experts" Session-Are Sports Nutrition Guidelines Too Elite Focused for Recreational Athletes?
abstract: This article provides a synopsis of the 10 Questions/10 Experts session at the 2026 American College of Sports Medicine Annual Meeting, which examined whether sports nutrition guidelines are equally applicable from recreational to elite athletes. Each speaker considered the validity of a given common "myth" statement and provided an evidence-based opinion to support, bust, or qualify propositions addressing the following questions: (a) Are sports nutrition guidelines based primarily on studies of elite athletes, and are they too serious for recreational athletes? (b) Do recreational marathon runners need the same in-race carbohydrate recommendations as elite marathon runners? (c) Must recreational athletes consume 1.6 g·kg-1·day-1 of protein to benefit from exercise training? (d) Does nitrate supplementation benefit elite and recreational athletes equally? (e) Do recreational athletes need a structured fluid intake plan? (f) Is sodium bicarbonate loading relevant only to elite athletes? (g) Do recreational and elite athletes require more micronutrients than suggested by the Recommended Dietary Allowances? (h) Is eating after 8:00 p.m. detrimental to performance or recovery in recreational athletes? (i) Are recreational athletes at greater risk for suboptimal vitamin D status because indoor occupations reduce sunlight exposure? and (j) Should recreational athletes train with low carbohydrate availability to amplify adaptation? This article describes the content of each presentation, including the most important evidence, practical implications, and conclusions identified by the presenters.

title: Bilateral erector spinae and biceps femoris co-activation following unilateral hamstring injury in young sprinters.
abstract: This study compared coactivation and strength of the erector spinae (ES) and biceps femoris long head (BFLH) during isometric knee flexion and trunk extension in sprinters with a recent BFLH injury. Twenty-four sprinters with grade 2 BFLH injury and 21 controls performed prone trunk extension and knee flexion maximal voluntary contractions (MVCs) at 90° and 0° knee flexion. Torque and surface electromyography (EMG) of the ES and BFLH were recorded bilaterally and normalized to MVCs during 30° trunk extension and 0° knee flexion, respectively. Previously injured athletes showed a greater co-contraction index (CCI) during knee flexion at 0° and 90° than controls (p < 0.001), with higher ES activation (32.52 ± 17.08 to 47.72 ± 17.83% MVC) than the uninjured group (21.56 ± 14.52 to 44.68 ± 18.02% MVC; p < 0.05). No group differences were found in normalized BFLH EMG, CCI during trunk extension, or absolute knee flexion or trunk extension strength (p > 0.05). Previously injured sprinters showed larger between-limb knee flexion strength asymmetries (>10%, p < 0.01), which were absent in controls. This paraspinal overactivation and increased trunk-hamstring co-contraction after BFLH injury suggest that lumbopelvic control exercises may be beneficial for preventing BFLH re-injury.

title: Early-stage calcification promotes tendon damage under cyclic loading through alterations in interfascicular matrix viscoelastic properties.
abstract: Calcification is a prevalent condition that alters mechanical and structural properties of soft tissues. While significant efforts have been devoted to the characterization of tendon mechanics, little work has been done so far on understanding the impact of calcification on tissues such as tendons. In this work, we investigate the influence of cycling loading and forced fluid flow on the mechanical and structural properties of tendon fascicle bundles of varying interfascicular matrix (IFM) content at an early stage of calcification. The calcification process was modeled using sample incubation in concentrated simulated body fluid. To evaluate the biomechanical responses of the tendon over the course of calcification, we compared four sets of samples incubated for 7 days in simulated body fluid, forced fluid flow and under cyclic uniaxial loading against a non-incubated control. Mechanical and structural properties were investigated using uniaxial tests, scanning electron microscopy and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy. The study revealed that the initial phase of calcification causes an increase in the elasticity, as well as a drop in the normalized value of hysteresis for both IFM-rich and IFM-poor regions of the tendon. However, the relaxation behavior of the tissue remained unchanged during calcification proving that calcium phosphate deposits do not affect the IFM viscoplastic behavior but tissue viscoelasticity instead, which is manifested by a change in hysteresis. The greatest changes in stiffness are observed for statically incubated samples, while cyclically loaded samples were the most susceptible to fibril damage although they did not demonstrate the greatest increases in elastic modulus. The results presented in this work show that the calcification process modifies the collagen-matrix interactions, which leads to a change in their mechanical properties depending on the loading conditions. These findings contribute to our understanding of the pathogenesis of tendinopathy and have the potential to assist in the identification of effective treatment strategies for calcification-induced disorders.

title: Macrophages in rotator cuff injuries and tendon-to-bone healing: Heterogeneity, pathophysiology, and therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Rotator cuff tears (RCTs) are a leading cause of shoulder disability, with high postoperative failure rates primarily attributed to poor tendon-to-bone healing. Macrophages act as central regulators of the inflammatory and regenerative microenvironment in the injured enthesis, tendon stump, subacromial bursa, and rotator cuff musculature. This review highlights the spatiotemporal heterogeneity and phenotypic plasticity of macrophages revealed by single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. Rather than following a simple M1-to-M2 transition, macrophages adopt context-dependent inflammatory, resolving, remodeling, and profibrotic programs across different stages and tissue compartments of rotator cuff injury. Persistent inflammatory programs are associated with chronic inflammation, matrix degradation, fatty infiltration, and muscle atrophy, whereas resolving and reparative programs may support inflammation resolution and fibrocartilaginous regeneration; sustained remodeling or profibrotic states may also contribute to pathological fibrosis. The review further explores macrophage-stem cell crosstalk under mechanical loading and the contribution of dysregulated macrophage function to the progression of cuff tear arthropathy. Advanced strategies including stem cell-derived exosomes, immuno-engineered scaffolds, and targeted immunomodulation, have shown therapeutic potential in preclinical studies, but their clinical efficacy and translational applicability remain to be established.

title: Adipose-Derived Orthobiologics and Extracellular Vesicles in Foot and Ankle Surgery: Current Evidence and Clinical Limitations.
abstract: Interest in adipose-derived orthobiologics and extracellular vesicles (EVs) has expanded as clinicians seek minimally invasive treatments for musculoskeletal disorders. However, culture-expanded adipose-derived stromal cells, stromal vascular fraction, microfragmented adipose tissue (MFAT), and isolated EVs are biologically and regulatorily distinct products. This narrative review summarizes their biological rationale, processing, clinical evidence, regulatory considerations, and potential application in foot and ankle surgery. Randomized studies in knee osteoarthritis suggest that MFAT may provide symptomatic improvement, but it has not consistently demonstrated superiority over other orthobiologic injections, and the certainty of evidence remains low. Preclinical EV studies provide biological plausibility for effects on tendon healing, tendon-to-bone integration, and cartilage repair. However, substantial heterogeneity in cellular source, preparation, dose, and experimental model limits translation. Human orthopaedic EV evidence remains confined to early studies in knee osteoarthritis using placental or umbilical cord derived products, with limited and conflicting evidence of efficacy and no completed studies specific to the foot and ankle. No adipose-derived regenerative medicine or EV product is Food and Drug Administration-approved for an orthopaedic indication. Current evidence therefore does not support routine clinical use or claims of tissue regeneration. Standardized product characterization and well-designed comparative trials are required to establish safety, efficacy, and appropriate clinical applications.

title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.

title: Editorial Commentary: Want to Try Anterior Cruciate Ligament Repair? Maximize Your Chances of Success by Choosing the Right Anterior Cruciate Ligaments to Repair Rather Than Reconstruct.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) repair represents an attractive choice for certain patients because of a higher rate of return to sport as well as a potentially faster recovery time. Recent evidence has shown that younger age and synovial sheath integrity <50% are associated with increased risk of failure after arthroscopic ACL repair. This makes sense because the synovial sheath is responsible for providing blood supply and proprioceptive nerve endings to the ACL, as well as protection of the ligament from the degradative environment of synovial fluid. As with any procedure, indications are refined over time based on new evidence. Although I believe that ACL reconstruction will remain the gold standard for the treatment of ACL tears, I also believe that our rates of success with ACL repair will improve as indications are further refined over time.

title: Running-based rehabilitation does not improve muscle function after volumetric muscle loss despite improving hindlimb weight-bearing asymmetry in mice.
abstract: Volumetric muscle loss (VML) is a traumatic skeletal muscle injury characterized by chronic functional impairments in the affected muscle and adjacent uninjured bone. Rehabilitative strategies aimed at restoring limb function following VML, including voluntary running, have shown limited efficacy and in some cases have been detrimental. One potential explanation is disproportional loading of the uninjured contralateral limb during running, but evaluation of unilateral weight-bearing following VML has not been explored. This study was designed to evaluate if the limited response to rehabilitation following VML could be explained by limb loading asymmetry. Twelve-week-old C57Bl/6J mice (n = 24; equal males/females) were randomized to three groups: Naïve-Run, VML, and VML-Run. Two weeks post-VML, mice in running groups were provided free access to wheels for 6 weeks. Weight-bearing asymmetry was assessed before injury and biweekly thereafter. Terminally at ∼20 weeks of age, in vivo muscle function was evaluated, and muscles and bones were saved for analyses. Prior to injury, no difference in weight-bearing asymmetry was observed across groups. VML-injured mice exhibited similar weight-bearing asymmetries prior to running. Following 6 weeks of running, VML-Run mice regained weight-bearing symmetry comparable to Naïve-Run. Despite this, remaining muscle function remained persistently impaired following VML injury. Collectively this works suggests that voluntary running promotes favourable weight-bearing adaptations following VML, but does not improve muscle function or the mechanical properties of the adjacent bone.

title: Effects of anti-aging diets and exercise on age-related musculoskeletal diseases via gut microbiota modulation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This review summarizes evidence on how anti-aging diets and exercise influence age-related musculoskeletal diseases through modulation of the gut microbiota. With population aging, these diseases are public health concerns. The gut microbiota regulates bone, joint, and muscle health via the gut‑joint, gut‑bone, and gut‑muscle axis. Few reviews integrate diet-exercise synergy with mechanistic pathways linking microbial changes to tissue outcomes.
DISCUSSION: Anti‑aging dietary strategies, classified into caloric restriction (ketogenic diet, fasting‑mimicking diet, intermittent fasting, time‑restricted feeding) and isocaloric nutrient restriction (e.g. protein or amino acid restriction), reshape gut microbiota composition and function. Caloric restriction and intermittent fasting reduce inflammation and benefit joint and muscle health, whereas long‑term ketogenic or protein/amino acid restriction may adversely affect bone density and muscle anabolism. Moderate exercise increases microbial diversity, enriches beneficial taxa (Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium), and boosts short‑chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, especially butyrate. Exercise also strengthens intestinal barrier integrity, reduces lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑induced systemic inflammation, and alleviates osteoarthritis (OA), bone loss, and sarcopenia in preclinical models. Combined diet and exercise may provide greater benefits than either alone. However, most evidence derives from animal or small human studies, and causality remains unclear. Future research should clarify causal mechanisms via multi‑omics and germ‑free models.
CONCLUSION: This review suggests that both anti-aging diets and moderate exercise may improve age-related musculoskeletal diseases partly through gut microbiota modulation. Given substantial inter‑individual variability, future research should prioritize personalized nutrition and exercise prescriptions tailored to microbiota, genetic background, and lifestyle. These findings inform precision strategies to promote healthy aging.

title: Culturally Embedded Participation Restrictions in Indian Adults With Knee Osteoarthritis: An ICF-Based Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify culturally relevant functioning issues experienced by Indian adults with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured focus group interviews was conducted with 38 ambulatory adults (35-85 years) diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Participants were recruited from physiotherapy outpatient departments and community settings using maximum variation sampling. Interviews were conducted in Gujarati, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Meaningful concepts were systematically linked to ICF categories using established linking rules. Dual independent coding and consensus discussions ensured the analytic rigour.
RESULTS: This study included 38 participants with KOA. Fifty-five meaningful second-level categories were identified. The most represented components were activities and participation (41.2%) and body functions (29.4%). Frequently mapped first-level categories included mobility (n = 22), neuromusculoskeletal and movement-related functions (n = 9), d6 domestic life (n = 10), community, social and civic life (n = 7) and products and technology (n = 9). Sixteen additional categories not represented in the existing ICF Core Set for OA emerged, particularly relating to culturally embedded activities such as floor sitting, squatting for toileting and religious participation. Environmental barriers, including inaccessible infrastructure and limited rehabilitation services, influenced disability experience.
CONCLUSION: Functioning among Indian adults with KOA is influenced by culturally embedded participation demands and contextual barriers that are insufficiently captured in the existing ICF Core Set for osteoarthritis (OA). These findings provide preliminary empirical support for contextual validation of the ICF Core Set for OA and inform potential culturally responsive adaptation for KOA.

title: Anatomic feasibility of using Shark Screw tendon for humeral ligament re-construction in medial and posterolateral elbow instability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medial and posterolateral rotational instability of the elbow, often resulting from collateral ligament insufficiency, can lead to pain and functional impairment. Surgical re-construction is indicated when conservative treatment fails, yet complications such as graft failure and donor-site morbidity persist. This study investigates the anatomic and biomechanical feasibility of the Shark Screw tendon as a representative human allogeneic bone screw for humeral ligament fixation in cases of elbow instability.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen cadaveric specimens were used to evaluate the feasibility of the use of a Shark Screw tendon for humeral fixation on both medial and lateral sides. Cyclic loading and failure testing were performed to assess time-zero fixation characteristics and failure load.
RESULTS: A total of sixteen testing scenarios were conducted on the specimens. Implantation was technically feasible without anatomic limitations related to implant size or positioning. Six graft failures occurred (38%), all attributable to poor tissue quality. Tendon slippage was observed in 9 of 16 cases (56%) under progressively increasing axial load, while the Shark Screw tendon remained seated. The mean failure load was 101 N (±50) for medial insertions, 118 N (±77) for lateral insertions, and 110 N (±64) overall. After 100 cycles, tendon displacement averaged 1.1 mm (±0.4) during extension-flexion on the medial side, 1.0 mm (±1.0) on the lateral side, and 1.0 mm (±0.7) overall. During supination-pronation, displacement was 0.8 mm (±0.7) medially, 1.0 mm (±0.8) laterally, and 0.9 mm (±0.7) overall. No anchor pullout was observed, although one anchor tip fractured during insertion.
CONCLUSION: The Shark Screw tendon appears to be a feasible biologically integrative alternative for humeral fixation in medial and posterolateral elbow ligament re-construction, demonstrating preliminary time-zero fixation characteristics in a cadaveric model. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes.

title: Bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses to short-term low energy availability with and without preserved protein intake: a randomized, controlled, multi-period, cross-over trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Bone appears sensitive to low energy availability (LEA), with prolonged exposure linked to compromised bone health. Causality, however, along with underlying mechanisms, and the role of macronutrient availability remain unclear.
PURPOSE: To investigate the influence of short-term energy and protein manipulation on bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses to acute exercise.
METHODS: Nineteen healthy, active young adults (9 females, 10 males) completed three 5-day dietary conditions in a randomized crossover design: adequate energy availability (AEA; 45 kcal·kgFFM·day-1), LEA (15 kcal·kgFFM·day-1) and LEA with protein matched to AEA (LEA-P). On days 1 and 5, participants completed a standardized exercise protocol comprising 45 min of cycling at 65% of pre-defined peak power output followed by a Wingate test, with blood samples collected at prespecified time-points to assess fasted and post-exercise bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses.
RESULTS: Fasted P1NP was lower following both energy-restricted trials compared with AEA, and remained lower during post-exercise recovery following LEA-P. CTX-1 was higher in the post-exercise recovery period following LEA-P only. Multiple inflammatory cytokines (IL6, IL8, IL10, ILRa, and IL1β) increased at distinct time-points in both energy-restricted trials. Overall, evidence for condition effects relative to AEA was more consistent following LEA-P than LEA.
CONCLUSION: Short-term energy restriction suppressed biomarkers indicative of bone formation and augmented the inflammatory cytokine response to exercise, with some, but less consistent evidence for increased bone resorption. Preserving protein intake did not attenuate these effects. In contrast, this condition was associated with more consistent and pronounced perturbations, potentially reflecting reduced carbohydrate availability rather than protein per se.

title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions.
METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot.
RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance.
CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.

title: Effects of muscle length and age on neuromuscular responses to maximal eccentric contractions of the plantar flexors.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Eccentric contractions induce greater neuromuscular impairment and muscle damage than concentric contractions. Muscle length is a key modulator of these responses, yet the combined effects of eccentric contractions and muscle length on neuromuscular function in older adults remain unclear. We investigated acute and delayed neuromuscular responses to eccentric plantar flexor contractions performed at different muscle lengths in young and older adults.
METHODS: Twenty-four young and 26 older adults performed 10 sets of 10 maximal eccentric plantar flexor contractions at either short (30°-0° plantar flexion) or long (0°-30° dorsiflexion) muscle lengths (12 young and 13 older adults per condition). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, voluntary activation, and evoked responses (100 Hz and 10 Hz doublets) were measured before, immediately after, and 1, 24, and 48 h post-exercise. Changes were compared between groups and conditions.
RESULTS: Despite similar torque-time integrals between young and older adults within the same muscle length condition, a muscle length effect was only found in young adults, with a greater (p = 0.021) MVIC decrease at long (-33.6 ± 13.2%) than short lengths (-8.4 ± 15.7%). Older adults showed similar reductions across conditions (≈ - 14-21%). Voluntary activation decreased only at long lengths, with no age difference. Evoked responses showed an age effect (p = 0.032), and the 10/100 Hz ratio decreased only in young after long muscle lengths. Neuromuscular function returned to baseline within 24 h indicating no evidence of severe alteration, although muscle soreness remained elevated at 48 h.
CONCLUSION: Long muscle length eccentric contractions induced greater force loss in young but not older adults, with no evidence of prolonged functional impairment in healthy, physically active older adults.

title: The Effect of Training Exercise on Cartilage Zonal Composition and Structure at Two Differently Loaded Sites in the Juvenile Equine Metacarpophalangeal Joint.
abstract: BackgroundThe aim of this study was to investigate the depth related spatial distribution of biochemical and structural components in articular cartilage at different topographical sites experiencing different loading within the juvenile equine metacarpophalangeal joint in two groups of foals subjected to different exercise conditions.MethodsSixteen Warmblood foals were included in the study and were randomly assigned into 1 of 2 exercise groups (box rest and box rest plus training) during the first 5 months of life and subsequently euthanized. Osteochondral plugs were harvested from two sites which have previously been shown to experience different load levels and sectioned into 100 μm thick slices. Cartilage slices were analysed for glycosaminoglycan, DNA, and total collagen content, as well as content of hydroxylysine residues (HYL) in collagen and the collagen cross-link Hydroxylysylpyridinoline (HP). Collagen fibril architecture (Orientation Angle and Parallelism Index) was determined using quantitative polarized light microscopy.ResultsThe constantly loaded site 2 exhibited higher glycosaminoglycan (GAG) and HP content with HYL higher in the superficial and middle layers of the trained group, while the intermittently peak loaded site 1 showed greater collagen accumulation in deeper layers but lower cross-link density. Structural analyses (Oa and PI) confirmed that collagen fibril orientation and alignment adapt regionally, with training enhancing fibril organization in superficial zones.ConclusionThis study illustrates that mechanical loading is a key driver of functional adaptation, resulting in distinct zonal and topographical differences in the biochemical and structural composition of equine cartilage at 5 months.

title: A wearable vibroarthrography system with PID-controlled negative-pressure suction and synchronized posture estimation.
abstract: BackgroundVibroarthrography (VAG) is a non-invasive technique for evaluating joint health through acoustic signals generated during movement. However, reliable signal acquisition during dynamic activities remains challenging due to sensor displacement, motion artifacts, and inconsistent skin contact.ObjectiveThis study proposes an advanced wearable VAG system integrating PID-controlled negative-pressure suction and real-time posture estimation to improve signal stability and enhance the assessment of knee joint mechanics during movement.MethodsThe proposed system combines a wearable acoustic sensing module with a vacuum-assisted suction cup and a PID controller that consistently maintains sensor adhesion. Real-time posture estimation is achieved using MediaPipe Pose, which computes knee flexion angles. VAG signals and kinematic data are synchronously acquired during OKC and CKC exercises for integrated analysis.ResultsIn this single-subject pilot test, the system achieved stable sensor attachment and repeatable vibroacoustic recordings throughout dynamic movements. Distinguishable frequency-domain characteristics were observed at relevant knee flexion angles, including approximately 30°, 63°, and 129°.ConclusionsThis pilot feasibility study demonstrates that the proposed wearable VAG platform can achieve stable acquisition of synchronized vibroacoustic and kinematic signals during dynamic knee movement in a single subject. These preliminary findings suggest potential future applications in osteoarthritis screening, rehabilitation assessment, and ambulatory monitoring, pending validation in larger, statistically powered cohorts.

title: Heart-to-kidney signal by extracellular vesicles promotes kidney injury in cardiorenal syndrome.
abstract:
AIMS: Cardiorenal syndrome type-1 (CRS1), defined as acute kidney injury occurring in the setting of acute cardiac illness, is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Our objective was to determine whether extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from the injured heart localize to the kidneys and contribute to renal injury in CRS1, and to elucidate mechanisms by which cardiac-derived EVs mediate kidney damage.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Using cardiomyocyte-specific EV reporter mice, we characterized the release of cardiac-derived EVs and their biodistribution to the kidneys. Acute myocardial infarction increased circulating levels of these EVs and enhanced their uptake by proximal tubular epithelial cells. To directly assess their impact on the kidney, EVs derived from cardiomyocytes cultured under normoxic (N-EV) or hypoxic (H-EV) conditions were injected into the renal arteries of wild-type mice. H-EV, but not N-EV, induced proximal tubular epithelial cell injury and worsening of kidney function. To identify EV biomarkers, we performed proteomic profiling of cargo from N-EV and H-EV, and validated the muscle-specific protein TRIM72 as a biomarker of EVs originating from injured cardiomyocytes. In a porcine CRS1 model, plasma levels of TRIM72 positive-EVs were increased, and we demonstrate their delivery to the kidney. Similarly, in CRS1 patients, higher plasma levels of TRIM72-positive EVs correlated with the development of acute kidney injury. Mechanistically, uptake of H-EVs by proximal tubular epithelial cells induced transcription of lipogenic genes and caused lipid accumulation, whereas lipogenesis blockade protected these cells from H-EV-induced injury. We subsequently found that reduced expression of the transcription factor FOXO3 drove H-EV-induced transcriptomic reprogramming. H-EV cargo was enriched with specific Foxo3-targeting miRNAs, whose delivery promoted proximal tubular epithelial cell cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, and suppressed FOXO3 levels.
CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this work demonstrates that a Foxo3-targeting miRNA heart-to-kidney signal mediated by injured cardiac-derived EVs contributes to kidney injury in CRS1.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Osteoarthritis: A Review and Opportunities for Novel Therapeutics.
abstract: ➢ Osteoarthritis (OA) represents a biologically dynamic disease characterized by progressive failure of cartilage homeostasis through interconnected molecular mechanisms. Chondrocytes shift from an anabolic to a catabolic phenotype, marked by increased matrix metalloproteinase activity, while the synthetic capacity of articular cartilage diminishes.➢ Key signaling cascades including NF-κB (nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells) and MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) become dysregulated, driving matrix degradation. Declining autophagy impairs cellular quality control while senescent cells accumulate, releasing inflammatory mediators that amplify tissue damage. The immune response extends beyond macrophage polarization to involve adaptive immune cells, including T cell subsets that sustain chronic synovial inflammation.➢ Emerging disease-modifying strategies-including Wnt pathway inhibitors, FGF (fibroblast growth factor) 18 analogs, senolytic agents, gene therapy approaches, and allogeneic MSC (mesenchymal stem cell) implantation-offer the first genuine prospects for altering the natural history of this disease. However, translational challenges remain, as highlighted by mixed results in recent clinical trials.➢ The future of OA management lies in precision molecular orthopaedics: matching patients to targeted therapies on the basis of their predominant disease endotype.

title: Propionibacterium cheese and bone turnover in active young adults: a randomized-controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Young physically active individuals exposed to prolonged physiological stress and low energy availability are prone to reduced gonadal steroid protection and increased bone turnover. Nutritional strategies that favor positive bone remodeling balance are of clinical interest. Jarlsberg cheese contains Propionibacterium freudenreichii (PF), which produces vitamin K₂ and 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoic acid (DHNA), compounds with potential favorable effects on bone health.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this 24-week sex-stratified randomized-controlled trial, 60 young physically active adults engaged in endurance training were allocated to daily intake of either Jarlsberg cheese or a nutritionally comparable control cheese without PF. The primary outcome was change in serum total osteocalcin (tOC). Secondary outcomes were changes in carboxylated osteocalcin (cOC), procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP), cross-linked C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX), P1NP/CTX ratio, lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD), and trabecular bone score (TBS).
RESULTS: After 24 weeks, serum tOC was significantly higher in the Jarlsberg group than in controls (38.0 vs. 26.8 ng/mL, p < 0.01). cOC and P1NP/CTX ratio increased in favor of the Jarlsberg group (p = 0.03). Lumbar spine BMD increased in the Jarlsberg group (mean change 0.012 g/cm2, p = 0.03), with a greater increase than in controls (p = 0.05), and TBS showed a positive trend in the Jarlsberg group.
CONCLUSION: Daily intake of cheese-containing PF was associated with favorable changes in bone turnover markers and increase in lumbar spine BMD. These findings suggest that PF-fermented cheese may support bone metabolism in young individuals exposed to reduced hormonal protection and high bone turnover.

title: Reduction in Force Complexity Following Eccentric Exercise That Elicits Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Unaccustomed eccentric exercise has been shown to lead to muscle damage. Previous research suggests that fatigue reduces the complexity of muscle force output. However, previous research has not investigated whether the force complexity response to fatigue is affected by eccentric exercise. Therefore, the purpose of the present study was to examine the effect of eccentric exercise and a subsequent fatiguing task on force variability and complexity.
METHODS: Twelve individuals (six females) participated in the study. The participants performed eccentric exercise consisting of six sets of 10 repetitions of the knee extensors to elicit muscle damage. Before and 48 hr after eccentric exercise, the participants were assessed for maximal voluntary contraction and performed a sustained isometric time to task failure protocol at 25% of maximal voluntary contraction. Force variability was assessed in the first 10 s (Fresh) and last 10 s (End-Task) of the time to task failure via standard deviation, coefficient of variation, detrended fluctuation analysis, sample entropy, and multiscale sample entropy.
RESULTS: Maximal voluntary contraction (532.67 ± 177.49 N vs. 448.54 ± 186.92 N, p < .001) and time to task failure (197.10 ± 44.81 s vs. 157.70 ± 62.52 s, p = .031) were reduced after eccentric exercise. There were no differences in force variability following eccentric exercise at either the Fresh or End-Task time points. Force complexity was reduced at both Fresh (detrended fluctuation analysis: 1.37 ± 0.18 vs. 1.47 ± 0.21; sample entropy: 0.88 ± 0.27 vs. 0.71 ± 0.027) and End-Task (sample entropy: 0.63 ± 0.17 vs. 0.53 ± 0.15), following eccentric exercise compared with the pre-eccentric exercise condition.
CONCLUSIONS: Reductions in force complexity, but not force variability, were observed following eccentric exercise. These changes are thought to be due to changes in motor control strategies to compensate for damaged tissue.

title: Cell-Based Regenerative Strategies for Knee Cartilage Repair: A Scoping Review of Autologous Cartilage, Mesenchymal Stromal Cells, and Hybrid Approaches.
abstract: BackgroundCell-based approaches for focal knee cartilage repair include cartilage- and chondrocyte-based procedures, mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-based strategies, and combinations of these approaches. However, the amount and type of evidence available for these treatments differ considerably.ObjectiveTo map the clinical and preclinical evidence for cell-based regenerative strategies used for focal chondral and osteochondral defects of the knee, compare cartilage-based, MSC-based, and hybrid approaches, and identify areas where evidence remains limited.MethodsThis scoping review was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework and reported according to PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published from January 2000 to December 2025. Eligible studies evaluated in vivo cartilage-derived, MSC-based, or hybrid regenerative interventions for focal knee chondral or osteochondral defects. Two reviewers independently screened the records and charted study characteristics and outcomes using a standardized form. Because of substantial heterogeneity in interventions, study designs, models, outcomes, and follow-up periods, the findings were summarized descriptively rather than pooled.ResultsSeventy-five publications met the eligibility criteria. Cartilage-based approaches were evaluated in 29 publications, including 21 clinical and 8 preclinical studies. MSC-based approaches were evaluated in 43 publications, including 12 clinical and 31 preclinical studies. Three publications examined hybrid strategies, including two clinical reports from the same 35-patient cohort and one preclinical study. Cartilage-based evidence was therefore mainly clinical (72.4%), whereas MSC-based evidence was mainly preclinical (72.1%). Clinical studies used a wide range of outcome measures, and comparative studies did not show a consistent advantage of one more complex cell-based approach over another. Evidence for hybrid strategies remained limited to one preclinical study and one clinical programme reported at 18 months and 5 years.ConclusionThe available evidence differs considerably across cartilage-based, MSC-based, and hybrid approaches. Cartilage-based techniques have been studied more extensively in clinical settings, whereas most MSC research remains preclinical. Hybrid cartilage and MSC strategies have been investigated in only a small number of studies. A framework based on structural or chondrogenic input, biological signaling, and the combination of these components may be useful for organizing future research, but it should currently be considered a hypothesis rather than a validated treatment model.

title: Jiawei Duhuo Jisheng Mixture Attenuates H2O2-induced Oxidative Injury and Osteogenic Dysfunction in Primary Osteoblasts: An Integrated Target Analysis and Experimental Validation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Oxidative stress-induced osteoblast dysfunction is an important event in osteoporosis (OP). Jiawei Duhuo Jisheng Mixture (JDJM) is clinically used for bone-related disorders, but its molecular basis in OP remains unclear. This study explored OP-related candidate targets of JDJM and evaluated its cytoprotective effects in a hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-induced primary osteoblast injury model.
METHODS: Candidate JDJM targets were predicted from its identified constituents and intersected with OP-related genes. The study integrated network-based and enrichment analyses with single-cell mapping, followed by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation. An H2O2-induced primary osteoblast injury model was used for experimental validation.
RESULTS: A total of 210 shared targets were identified. Network pharmacology and enrichment analyses implicated JDJM in the regulation of oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, extracellular matrix remodelling, osteogenesis and apoptosis, primarily through the MAPK, JAK-STAT and PI3K-Akt signalling pathways. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further localized these candidate targets to osteogenic, stromal, vascular, and inflammatory cell populations. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations predicted stable interactions between representative JDJM-derived compounds and selected protein targets. In H2O2-injured primary osteoblasts, JDJM significantly reduced mean DCF fluorescence intensity, increased the alkaline phosphatase (ALP)-positive area and Alizarin Red S absorbance, and partially restored osteocalcin/bone Gla protein (OCN/BGP) protein and Bglap mRNA expression.JDJM was also associated with decreased total JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, and Bad expression and partial restoration of ESR1 expression.
DISCUSSION: JDJM attenuated H2O2-induced oxidative injury and osteogenic dysfunction in primary osteoblasts, accompanied by changes in JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, ESR1, and Bad expression. These results support a multi-target cytoprotective effect of JDJM under oxidative-stress conditions, although direct regulation of the corresponding signaling pathways remains to be confirmed.
CONCLUSION: JDJM attenuated H2O2-induced oxidative injury and partially restored osteogenic function in primary osteoblasts, accompanied by coordinated expression changes in JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, ESR1, and Bad. These findings support a multi-target protective effect of JDJM against oxidative stress-related osteoblast dysfunction.

title: Radial pressure wave treatment accelerates recovery from immobilization-induced soleus muscle atrophy and improves ankle range of motion in mice.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Disuse muscle atrophy following immobilization is characterized by decreased muscle mass and reduced joint range of motion (ROM). Radial pressure wave (RPW) treatment is a non-invasive modality that delivers mechanical energy to musculoskeletal tissues, but its efficacy in skeletal muscle recovery from disuse atrophy remains largely unknown. We examined whether RPW treatment accelerates soleus muscle structural recovery and passive ankle dorsiflexion ROM following immobilization-induced atrophy in mice. Furthermore, we investigated the underlying molecular signaling cascades and gene expression profiles associated with RPW-mediated recovery.

title: Creative Solution for Recurrent Failure of Flexor Tendon Repair.
abstract: Flexor tendon injuries present complex surgical and rehabilitative challenges, particularly in zone 2 of the hand. Despite multiple complications, including recurrent ruptures and repair failures, the case underscores the importance of individualized surgical planning, coordinated rehabilitation, and shared decision-making in achieving optimal functional recovery.

title: Examining the Impact of Supramaximal Eccentric and Long-Lever Isometric Training Protocols on Isometric Hamstring Strength, Nordic Hamstring Performance, and Sprint Speed.
abstract: The aim of this study was to compare the effects of a 6-week higher-volume eccentric training protocol with a combined lower-volume eccentric and long-lever isometric protocol on posterior chain strength and sprint performance. Thirty-three NCAA Division II soccer players (men: n = 17, age = 19.7 ± 1.2 years, height = 178.9 ± 6.6 cm, body mass 79.8 ± 8.1 kg; women: n = 16, age = 20.1 ± 0.9 years, height = 166.7 ± 5.2 cm, body mass = 67.0 ± 12.1 kg) were allocated to either group via exhaustive minimization. Nordic hamstring exercise break-point angle (NBPA), rapid isometric hamstring strength (LLB), 20m sprint performance, and continuous angular knee extension velocity waveforms were assessed pre- and post-intervention, and following a 2-week detraining period. A significant main effect of time was observed for sprint, NBPA, and rapid isometric strength (p < 0.05); however, Bonferroni-corrected within-group comparisons reached significance only for sprint performance in both groups, with no significant between-group differences for any outcome. Equivalence testing supported comparable sprint adaptations between protocols but could not be established for eccentric or isometric hamstring strength. All discrete outcome measures were largely maintained or continued to develop following the detraining period though range-specific eccentric strength appeared more sensitive to the training cessation. A combined low-volume eccentric and isometric training approach may represent a viable alternative to higher-volume eccentric programming for hamstring strength and speed development, although this should be approached cautiously to preserve neuromuscular qualities relevant to hamstring injury risk mitigation.

title: A distributed event-triggered framework for coordinating athlete autonomic states via wearable sensor networks.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Interpersonal autonomic physiology (IAP) research has established that physiological synchrony (PS), the temporal interdependence of autonomic nervous system (ANS) activity across individuals, is an established phenomenon in team-based settings. However, PS in athlete cohorts has been studied exclusively as a passive observational variable; no framework actively regulates autonomic coherence under the communication constraints of wireless body area networks. This study integrates IAP and distributed control theory by formulating team-level autonomic coherence as a leaderless multi-agent consensus problem.
METHODS: Each wearable unit was modeled as a two-dimensional linear agent whose state encodes cardiovascular autonomic tone (parasympathetic index: HRV-RMSSD) and sympathetic arousal load (EDA skin-conductance level, SCL), consistent with the Banister Fitness-Fatigue Model. Initial model states were derived from ECG/EDA records of WESAD subjects S2-S7, used only to provide heterogeneous simulation initial conditions (correlations were directional, non-significant sanity checks: r = -0.71, p = 0.114 for RMSSD; r = 0.68, p = 0.137 for SCL; N = 6). Three engineering challenges were addressed: (i) BLE communication delays h c ∈ [15, 150] ms; (ii) neuromuscular input delays h i ∈ [150, 300] ms; and (iii) switching directed topologies from dynamic team formations. A distributed dynamic event-triggered mechanism (DETM) drove all agents toward consensus while transmitting data only upon detection of meaningful state deviation. Stability was established via a dual-integral Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional, with LMI feasibility verified by CVXPY (ε = 0.087). Simulations ran for 300 s under three delay scenarios with five initial-condition perturbation folds; battery life was estimated from a four-component nRF52840 energy model.
RESULTS: The proposed DETM reduced BLE transmissions by 38.38% in the nominal case while achieving convergence of the normalized model states within 4-7 s. A Zeno-free guarantee (T min = 0.06 s) and a theoretical battery-life estimate of about 36 days were obtained. The ablation analysis attributed the largest communication saving to the dynamic internal variable ρ i (t) and the largest convergence-time improvement to the dual-delay structure. Five initial-condition perturbation folds indicated numerical robustness to the starting states.
DISCUSSION: These findings support control-theoretic and network-level feasibility only. Athlete studies are required before physiological benefits, safety, or real-world effectiveness can be inferred.

title: A rare traumatic triad: Open bicondylar non-conjoint Hoffa fracture with partial tibial tubercle and medial epicondyle avulsions - A case report and biomechanical analysis.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Coronal shear fractures of the distal femoral condyles are rare intra-articular injuries, and the simultaneous occurrence of a non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture with a partial anterior tibial tubercle avulsion and a medial epicondyle avulsion constitutes an exceptionally complex traumatic triad. We report the case of a 35-year-old male motorcyclist who sustained this "floating" articular block injury (AO/OTA 33-B3.3) following a high-velocity accident. Diagnostic assessment utilizing Computed Tomography with 3D reconstruction revealed a vertical Letenneur Type II fracture of the medial condyle and a comminuted Letenneur Type I fracture of the lateral condyle, complicated by significant rotational instability. Surgical management prioritized the posterior femoral instability through a double posterior approach, which allowed for direct visualization and anatomical reduction. Fixation was achieved using posterior-to-anterior headless compression screws, augmented by a posterior buttress plate on the lateral column to neutralize shear forces, while the medial epicondyle was anatomically reduced and fixed; the stable partial tibial tubercle avulsion was treated conservatively. At the two-year follow-up, the patient demonstrated excellent functional recovery with 120 degrees of flexion, a Lysholm score of 91, and a successful return to recreational sports. This case highlights the importance of the double posterior approach and "targeted rigidity" in managing multidirectional instability, permitting early mobilization even in the presence of complex extensor mechanism involvement.
INTRODUCTION: Coronal shear fractures of the distal femoral condyles (Hoffa fractures) are rare intra-articular injuries, with bicondylar patterns being exceptionally uncommon. A non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture combined with a partial anterior tibial tubercle (ATT) avulsion and a medial epicondyle avulsion represents a complex, "floating" articular block that challenges standard treatment algorithms. This case report analyzes the biomechanics and management of this rare traumatic triad.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 35-year-old male motorcyclist presented with a Gustilo-Anderson Type I open knee injury following a high-velocity crash involving hyper-flexion and valgus stress. CT imaging confirmed a non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture (AO/OTA 33-B3.3, Bagaria Type 3). The lateral condyle presented as a Letenneur Type I fracture with extensive comminution, while the medial condyle was a Letenneur Type II vertical fracture. Associated injuries included an Ogden Type I partial ATT avulsion and a Watson-Jones Type I medial epicondyle avulsion.Surgical management utilized a double posterior approach to visualize and reduce the posterior fragments. Fixation involved headless cannulated compression screws for both condyles, augmented by a posterior buttress plate on the lateral column to resist shear forces. The medial epicondyle was refixed with a screw and washer, while the stable ATT avulsion was managed conservatively. At the two-year follow-up, the patient achieved excellent functional outcomes, including 120° of flexion, a Lysholm score of 91, and a Tegner Activity Scale score of 7.
CONCLUSION: Managing this complex triad requires a thorough understanding of the injury mechanism, which involves coronal shear, valgus stress, and eccentric extensor loading. 3D CT reconstruction is mandatory for planning, and a double posterior approach provides superior visualization for anatomical reduction and posterior-to-anterior fixation. Rigid fixation, particularly using anti-glide plating for the lateral column, permits early mobilization and the conservative management of stable associated injuries, leading to high patient satisfaction.

title: Medical Therapies for the Treatment of Osteoarthritis in the Horse - 20 years later….
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a debilitating joint disease, characterized by a degenerative catabolic cascade resulting in detrimental changes to all aspects of the joint including the irreversible destruction of articular cartilage. In 2006, a narrative review by Goodrich and Nixon outlined the available treatments for the medical management of OA; however, since that time substantial progress has been made. In recent years the therapeutic options for veterinarians managing horses with OA has increased significantly with a multitude of products available on the market. While many of the conventional treatments remain in clinical use, ongoing research continues to refine their application and evaluate their efficacy. Since their introduction, orthobiologic therapeutics have undergone extensive development, resulting in the emergence of numerous allogenic and autologous therapeutics. Similarly, cellular based therapies have advanced considerably. Overall, these advancements reflect a broader shift in treatment from those aimed predominantly at symptom management to interventions designed to modify the OA disease process. This narrative review follows up on the past 20 years of progress, outlining current evidence-based recommendations to provide a comprehensive guide for clinicians selecting therapeutic agents to treat horses with OA.

title: 660 nm LED preconditioning programs mitochondrial signaling in BMSCs for functional tracheal cartilage regeneration.
abstract: Stem-cell-based cartilage regeneration is limited not only by cell delivery, but also by the difficulty of establishing a stable and functionally competent regenerative cell state before implantation. Here, we report a photonic mitochondrial programming strategy in which 660 nm light-emitting diode (LED) irradiation preconditions bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) to enhance functional tracheal cartilage regeneration. BMSCs were seeded onto egg white-derived ring-shaped porous scaffolds and exposed to defined 660 nm LED irradiation before implantation. Among the tested irradiation conditions, 15 J/cm2 optimally promoted BMSC proliferation, chondrogenic differentiation and cartilage-like extracellular matrix deposition, while suppressing fibrotic, hypertrophic and matrix-degrading phenotypes. Mechanistically, 660 nm LED irradiation enhanced cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) activity, mitochondrial membrane potential, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production and respiratory function, accompanied by moderate reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling. This mitochondrial bioenergetic-redox response activated the PI3K/Akt/mTOR/GSK3β-SOX9 axis, thereby promoting type II collagen, aggrecan and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix formation. Pharmacological inhibition of ROS signaling, mitochondrial activity, PI3K or mTOR attenuated the LED-induced chondrogenic program. In a rabbit tracheal cartilage ring defect model, 15 J/cm2-preconditioned BMSC-scaffold constructs improved cartilage-like tissue formation, airway epithelial repair, lumen patency and mechanical support after 30 days of observation. These findings support 660 nm LED irradiation as a controllable mitochondrial preconditioning strategy for stem-cell-based functional cartilage regeneration.

title: The associations among athlete status, sleep, and well-being in a large national sample of college students.
abstract: Objective: College students, specifically student athletes, experience environments that can support and create barriers to flourishing, a form of well-being reflecting positive functioning in relationships, self-esteem, purpose, and optimism. Sleep is one factor that can have implications for student athletes' flourishing. This study explored whether sleep characteristics, including duration, quality, and napping, accounted for part of the association between athlete status and flourishing, as measured using the eight-item Flourishing Scale. Participants: Using the Fall 2022 National College Health Assessment (N = 28,608), structural equation models assessed these associations. Results: Compared with non-athletes, athletes reported better sleep quality, smaller weekday-weekend differences in sleep duration, and longer sleep duration. Athletes also reported more frequent and longer naps. These sleep factors were associated with flourishing although indirect associations were small (β < .06). Conculsion: Overall, athletes reported several favorable sleep characteristics relative to non-athletes, alongside more frequent and longer naps. Sleep remains important in understanding student athletes' flourishing.

title: Advances in disease management and treatment outcomes for obesity and knee osteoarthritis in primary care practice.
abstract: The lifetime risk of developing knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is approximately doubled in people with obesity compared with those without obesity. Many patients with KOA are treated by primary care physicians in the community setting. We performed a targeted literature search on PubMed to identify relevant literature describing the impact of weight loss in patients with obesity and KOA. A strong body of evidence supports the use of weight loss through lifestyle interventions, including caloric restriction in combination with exercise, as a primary intervention in patients with KOA and obesity. Studies show that these interventions are associated with improvements in pain, physical function, and quality of life; however, adherence to lifestyle interventions can be challenging, even with individually tailored programs. Obesity medications, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, are emerging as a new addition to weight management approaches in KOA, with a recent phase 3 clinical study demonstrating the benefits of semaglutide for weight loss in adults with KOA and high body mass index. Although initial data are promising, further clinical evidence is required, and perceived barriers to use need to be addressed before obesity medications can be widely adopted into clinical practice for patients with KOA. Specifically, further data are required to guide decisions regarding optimal treatment duration with obesity medications and to establish their tolerability profile associated with longer-term use. The importance of preserving functional muscle mass in patients with KOA and mitigation of weight regain after obesity medication treatment withdrawal are also identified as areas warranting further research. In this narrative review, we provide practical recommendations to primary care physicians on integrating obesity medications into weight-loss programs, including patient screening, risk stratification, communication, use of guidelines, and the benefits of a multidisciplinary approach.

title: Cartilage-targeting engineered probiotic bacterial extracellular vesicles treat osteoarthritis through modulation of matrix homeostasis.
abstract: Reversing extracellular matrix (ECM) metabolic dysregulation to facilitate cartilage repair represents a key therapeutic strategy for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment. Owing to the avascular nature of joint structures, intra-articular injection is a commonly used clinical administration route. However, the current drug retention time is insufficient to effectively reverse OA progression. In this study, we demonstrated that natural bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are capable of repairing cartilage damage. We modified Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)-derived BEVs with a chondrocyte-targeting peptide to prolong their therapeutic efficacy. Engineered BEVs, as a drug delivery system, are capable of continuously transporting endogenous miRNAs. Cartilage-targeting LGG-EVs (W-LGG-EVs) penetrate deeply into cartilage tissue and promote extracellular matrix secretion by chondrocytes. Furthermore, W-LGG-EVs were shown to restore cartilage homeostasis and ultimately alleviate stress-related OA. BEVs, as a novel and safe therapeutic agent, hold clinical feasibility.

title: Extreme energy expenditure during a 200 km three-day open-water swim: A doubly labeled water case study.
abstract: The upper limits of total energy expenditure (TEE) in humans have primarily been described during single-day ultra-endurance events, or during multistage land-based endurance events across several days. However, little is known about the physiological limits of sustained energy turnover during shorter multi-day, near-continuous exercise events, particularly when performed in an aquatic environment. Prolonged immersion in water imposes substantial thermoregulatory demands due to increased conductive heat loss, which may further elevate metabolic requirements beyond those observed in (cold) land-based events. The 200 km Elfstedentocht swim, completed over approximately three days with minimal sleep and near-continuous swimming, provides a unique opportunity to investigate the upper limits of human energy expenditure during prolonged multi-day exercise in water. In this case study, we therefore assessed TEE in a former Olympic athlete (mass 103 kg, height 2.04 m, age 38 years) during a 200-km swim completed over 3 days using doubly labeled water. TEE was 195 Megajoule (MJ) (46,700 kcals), corresponding to 6.17x basal metabolic rate over the three-day period. This TEE is among the highest TEE reported thus far over similar periods, suggesting that the combined near-continuous exercise and imposed sustained thermoregulatory demands due to conductive heat loss lead to extreme energy expenditure. Notably, the absolute energy expenditure of ∼14,700 kcal per day exceeds previous limits.

title: Are both hemolysis and impaired myocyte integrity associated with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
abstract: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is a potent antioxidant enzyme. G6PD deficiency, predominant among males, is a neonatal "neurotoxic" risk, characterized by episodic hemolysis that is sometimes infection triggered. Clinical risk among heterozygous G6PD-deficient females is often under-recognized. Recent reports of rhabdomyolysis among G6PD-deficient individuals are reviewed here. In one case, a male athlete with G6PD deficiency (<10% activity) experienced multiple, acute episodes of rhabdomyolysis, painful muscle symptomatology, injury and hemolysis after strenuous exertion. Both his mother with G6PD-deficiency (<45% activity) and maternal grandmother have chronic histories of episodic or triggered fatigue-related disruptive symptoms. Other case reports of G6PD-deficient individuals with muscle injury and exertional symptoms (with or without hemolysis) showed unique laboratory findings of elevated creatine kinase, myoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, and aminotransferases levels and myoglobinuria. Disrupted myocyte energetics and loss of cellular integrity can be attributed to impaired downstream pentose phosphate pathway (PPP)-related oxidant stress protection, which is a key enzymatic consequence of G6PD-deficiency. These triggered stresses may explain the muscle fatigue and propensity to exertional injury. Correlation between stress-sensitive-impaired muscle injury among all G6PD-deficient individuals, including neonates, requires further clinical validation to ascertain oxidant-stress impact of impaired PPP-dependent cellular energetics of red blood, white blood, neural, and muscle cells.

title: Extracellular vesicles and immune-glial remodeling in lung cancer brain metastasis: potential intersections with exercise-related myokines.
abstract: Lung cancer brain metastasis develops through reciprocal interactions between metastatic tumor cells and a brain-specific vascular, glial, and immune microenvironment. Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) can participate in this process by altering blood-brain barrier (BBB) properties, influencing brain-directed distribution, and transferring regulatory cargo to endothelial and myeloid recipient cells. This review integrates direct evidence from non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) brain or central nervous system metastasis with related lung cancer EV studies, while distinguishing these findings from cross-cancer mechanistic evidence. We first describe the transition from the BBB to the heterogeneous blood-tumor barrier and distinguish the contributions of astrocytes, resident microglia, recruited monocyte-derived macrophages, and T cells. We then examine how defined EV cargo, including lnc-MMP2-2, LINC00482, miR-21, L1CAM, and miR-374a-5p, affects barrier integrity, myeloid state, or brain-metastatic behavior. Myeloid responses are interpreted according to cellular origin and function rather than by a fixed M1/M2 binary. Exercise-related myokines and exerkines are considered separately as a hypothesis-generating systemic layer that could influence tumor-cell EV production, deliver signals through muscle-derived EVs, or alter recipient-cell responsiveness; none of these routes has yet been established as a causal mechanism in lung cancer brain metastasis. Together, current evidence supports a role for EV-mediated vascular and immune/glial communication in lung cancer brain metastasis, while leaving the contribution of exercise-related signals unresolved.

title: Extracellular vesicles: Multi-source regulatory mechanisms in hippocampal homeostasis.
abstract: Hippocampal health is pivotal for memory, emotional regulation, and cognition. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) facilitate intercellular and inter-organ communication by transporting bioactive cargos; however, traditional research often overlooks systemic influences on the hippocampus in favor of local microenvironmental changes. This review synthesizes evidence demonstrating that hippocampal homeostasis is modulated by the organism's systemic state-including aging, obesity, and immune status-via EVs. We detail mechanisms by which EVs from peripheral organs (adipose tissue, gut/microbiota, lung, bone, muscle, liver, kidney, heart, and spleen) and central nervous system resident cells (neurons, microglia, astrocytes, neural stem cells, and endothelial cells) regulate hippocampal function. These multi-source EVs precisely modulate neurogenesis, inflammatory responses, and synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, we highlight the emerging role of migrasomes as a specialized subset of EVs in this regulatory landscape. By mapping this comprehensive EV-mediated network, we provide a holistic perspective on the crosstalk between the systemic environment and the hippocampus, offering novel insights and therapeutic strategies for diseases associated with hippocampal dysfunction.
